name: Design Patterns in Java

topics.name: Singleton Pattern

beginner.content:
Singleton Pattern ensures that only one object of a class is created in the entire application.

Real-Life Example:

  • Database Connection
  • Printer Spooler
  • Configuration Manager

Why do we need Singleton?

  • To save memory
  • To maintain global access
  • To control object creation

Basic Rules:

  • Private constructor
  • Static instance variable
  • Public static method to get instance

In one minute

A Singleton is a class that allows exactly one object to exist, and gives everybody the same global access point to it. You hide the constructor (private constructor), keep the single object in a static field, and hand it out through a getInstance() method. Whoever asks gets the same object.

Real-life analogies

  • The Principal of a school: many students, one principal. Anyone who says "the principal" means the same person.
  • The ticket window of a fort: if every visitor opened a new window, the counts would never add up. One window keeps one running total.
  • The national flag at the Red Fort: there is one flag on the mast; everybody looks at the same one.

Where you see it in Java, the JDK and Spring

  • java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime() always returns the same Runtime object of the JVM.
  • java.awt.Desktop.getDesktop() and java.lang.System (static, one per JVM).
  • Spring beans are singleton scoped by default: one object per ApplicationContext (managed by the container, not by a private constructor).
  • Logger factories such as LogManager and enum constants are one-instance-per-JVM by design.

Structure (text diagram)

+--------------------------------+
|           Singleton            |
+--------------------------------+
| - instance : Singleton  (static)|
| - Singleton()           (private)|
+--------------------------------+
| + getInstance() : Singleton    |
+--------------------------------+
      ^           ^           ^
      |           |           |
   Client A    Client B    Client C   --> all receive the SAME object

When to use

  • Exactly one object is a business rule: configuration, logger, cache, connection pool, ticket counter.
  • The object is expensive to build and safe to share.

When NOT to use

  • When you only want "easy access to something" - a global variable in disguise hurts testing.
  • When the object holds per-user or per-request data (it would be shared by everyone).
  • When you can simply pass the object as a constructor argument (dependency injection).

Sample 1 - An app settings holder (eager singleton)

This version creates the object eagerly, when the class loads. It is the simplest thread-safe form because the JVM guarantees class loading happens once. Notice the == check: both variables point to the very same object.

Sample 2 - A visitor counter shared by two gates

Two different parts of the program (the "gates") never see each other, yet the total is correct because both talk to the one counter. This is the classic reason to use a Singleton. This version is lazy: the object is created on the first call, and synchronized keeps it safe.

intermediate.content:
The Singleton Pattern ensures that a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to it.

Why?

In the above program, we have created the 3 instance of same class but I want to create only 1 instance of class then I should go for singleton design pattern.

When?

If you have business requirement in which only 1 object is created then you should go for singleton design pattern.

Steps to create the singleton design pattern as

Step 1: Create class singleton and static member of class.
Step 2: Make constructor as private, so nobody outside the class can use new.
Step 3: Create the method for checking the references and use synchronized block instead of method.
Step 4: We can still create a copy of the object by cloning it with the object clone() method. If the singleton class implements Cloneable, cloning gives a second object. Run this program:
This again violates the design principle. To prevent cloning, override the object clone() method and throw CloneNotSupportedException. Calling super.clone() would NOT prevent cloning.

Singleton Pattern with Serialization

Some times in distributed system, we need to implement serializable interface in singleton class so that we can store its state in file system and retrieve it later point.

Step 1: Create the singleton class that implements Serializable.
Step 2: Create a test class that writes the object to a file and reads it back (serialize and deserialize). The input and output streams do the writing and reading (Step 3 is inside this program).

Step 4: Run the program to check the output. 
instance1 hashCode:- 625576447
instance2 hashCode:- 1494279232
It proves that the singleton object is not preserved during deserialization, because both instances have different hash codes.
Step 5: To overcome this problem, we need to override the readResolve() method into the singleton class.

Step 6: After running the SingletonSerializedTest program again, you will get the output as: 
instance1 hashCode:- 625576447
instance2 hashCode:- 625576447
Both hash codes are the same, so the singleton is preserved.

Variant 1 - Enum singleton

What it shows: a singleton written as an enum with one constant. Why: the JVM guarantees one instance, it is thread-safe, and it is immune to reflection and serialization attacks. Joshua Bloch calls this the best way to write a singleton in Java.

Variant 2 - Initialization-on-demand holder idiom

What it shows: a lazy singleton with no synchronized and no volatile. Why: the inner Holder class is loaded only when getInstance() is first called, and the JVM runs class initialisation exactly once and thread-safely. You get laziness and speed together.

Variant 3 - Double-checked locking with volatile

What it shows: a lazy singleton that locks only while the object does not exist yet. Why volatile: without it, another thread may see a half-constructed object because of instruction reordering. Four threads race here, but only one object is built.

Variant 4 - Singleton registry (one instance per key)

What it shows: a registry that keeps one object per name, created on demand. Why: sometimes you need "one per city" or "one per tenant", not one for the whole JVM. computeIfAbsent gives atomic creation.

Variant 5 - Surviving serialization with readResolve

What it shows: deserializing a singleton normally creates a second object. Why readResolve(): it lets you replace the freshly read object with the real singleton. (An enum does this for free.)

Common mistakes and how to avoid them

  • Lazy getInstance() without synchronization: two threads can both see null and build two objects. Use the holder idiom, an enum, or synchronized.
  • Double-checked locking without volatile: a thread may read a partly built object. Always declare the field volatile.
  • Mutable shared state with no protection: one instance does not make its fields thread-safe. Guard them or use concurrent collections.
  • Forgetting reflection and serialization: both can create a second object. Prefer an enum, or add readResolve() and throw from the constructor if the instance exists.
  • Hidden dependencies: calling X.getInstance() everywhere makes classes hard to unit-test. Inject it through a constructor instead.

Singleton vs Static class (comparison)

PointSingletonStatic utility class
Object exists?Yes, one objectNo object, only static methods
Implements interface / inheritanceYesNo
Lazy initialisationPossibleLoaded with the class
Can hold state per objectYesOnly static state
Easy to mock in testsYes, if behind an interfaceHard

expert.content:
Thread-Safe Singleton (Double Checked Locking)

This ensures only one instance is created even in multithreaded environment.

Bill Pugh Singleton Implementation (Best Practice)

Uses inner static helper class. Thread-safe without synchronized.

Singleton Using Enum (Most Secure Way)

✔ Prevents reflection attack
✔ Prevents serialization issue
✔ Prevents cloning issue
✔ Thread-safe by default

Common Singleton Issues & Solutions

  • Reflection: Can break singleton → Use enum
  • Serialization: Use readResolve()
  • Cloning: Override clone() method
  • Multithreading: Use Double Checked Locking or Bill Pugh

When NOT to use Singleton?

  • When dependency injection is better
  • When class has state changes frequently
  • When testing requires multiple instances

Real-time example 1 - Central logging service

A logging service is the textbook singleton: every class writes to the same sink, and the order of messages must be preserved. The log method is synchronized so concurrent callers do not interleave. In production you would use SLF4J/Logback, but the shape is identical.

Real-time example 2 - Configuration loader

Configuration is read once at start-up and then shared read-only. Loading in the constructor, making the map unmodifiable, and exposing typed getters keeps the singleton safe to share between threads without any locks.

Sample mini project - Fort ticket booking desk

One file, several small classes. The TicketDesk singleton issues unique ticket numbers and keeps the day's revenue, while separate Visitor and Ticket objects are ordinary. This is the realistic split: the singleton owns shared state, everything else stays normal.

Thread-safety, testing and Spring notes

  • Thread-safety: creation safety (enum, holder, DCL+volatile) is separate from state safety. A singleton that holds a mutable list needs synchronized, locks, or a concurrent collection.
  • Testing: a hard-coded getInstance() call cannot be replaced by a mock. Put an interface in front (Logger), pass it through the constructor, and let only the composition root call getInstance(). If you must reset state in tests, expose a package-private reset().
  • Spring: the default bean scope is singleton: one instance per container, created by Spring, no private constructor needed. Other scopes are prototype, request and session. Two containers (or class loaders) still give two instances, so "one per JVM" is not guaranteed.
  • Class loaders and clusters: in an application server or a multi-node cluster, "one instance" really means one per class loader / per node. Use a database or a distributed cache for truly global state.

Anti-patterns

  • God singleton: one class that does config, caching, logging and business logic.
  • Global mutable state: any class can change it, so bugs are impossible to trace.
  • Singleton as a service locator: classes pull their dependencies out of thin air, hiding what they need.
  • Lifetime leaks: a singleton that holds references to short-lived objects keeps them from being garbage-collected.

interviewQA: Which is the best way to implement a Singleton in Java?

An enum with a single constant: the JVM guarantees one instance, it is thread-safe and protects against reflection and serialization. If you need laziness with a normal class, use the initialization-on-demand holder idiom.
Why must the instance field be volatile in double-checked locking?
Without volatile the JVM may reorder the write of the reference before the constructor finishes, so another thread can see a non-null but half-built object. Volatile forbids that reordering.
How can a Singleton be broken, and how do you prevent it?

Reflection (setAccessible on the private constructor), serialization/deserialization, cloning, and multiple class loaders. Prevent with an enum, readResolve(), throwing from the constructor when an instance exists, and not implementing Cloneable.
What is the difference between a Singleton and a static class?
A singleton is a real object: it can implement interfaces, be passed around, be lazy and be mocked. A static class only has static members and cannot be polymorphic.
Is a Spring singleton bean the same as the Singleton pattern?

No. Spring creates one instance per ApplicationContext and per bean definition; the class itself can still be instantiated elsewhere. The GoF pattern enforces one instance per class loader through the class itself.
Why is Singleton often called an anti-pattern?

It is global state, it hides dependencies, it makes unit testing difficult and it couples classes to a concrete type. Dependency injection with a singleton-scoped object gives the benefit without the drawbacks.
Is the synchronized getInstance() a good solution?
It is correct but locks on every call, which costs under heavy contention. The holder idiom or an eagerly created static final instance avoids the lock entirely.

topics.name: Factory Design Pattern

beginner.content:
Factory Design Pattern is used to create objects without exposing object creation logic to the client.

Simple Meaning:

Instead of using new keyword everywhere, we create objects using a Factory class.


Why Factory Pattern?

  • Removes tight coupling
  • Centralizes object creation
  • Makes code cleaner

Basic Structure:

  • Step 1: Create Interface
  • Step 2: Create Concrete Classes
  • Step 3: Create Factory Class
  • Step 4: Call Factory from Client

Real Life Example:

Shape Factory → Circle, Rectangle, Square

In one minute

A Factory is a method (or class) whose only job is to create objects for you. The caller says what it needs ("sms"), the factory decides which class to build and returns it through a common interface. The client never writes new ConcreteClass(), so adding a new type does not change the client code.

Real-life analogies

  • A restaurant kitchen: you order "Paneer Tikka"; you do not go into the kitchen and cook it. The kitchen (factory) decides how it is made.
  • A vehicle showroom: you ask for "a scooter" and the showroom hands over a ready vehicle.
  • A courier counter: you say "express" or "normal" and the counter picks the right delivery process.

Where you see it in Java, the JDK and Spring

  • Calendar.getInstance(), NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance() and LocalDate.of(...) are static factory methods.
  • List.of(...), Optional.of(...), Integer.valueOf(...), Executors.newFixedThreadPool(...).
  • DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance() and Connection objects from DriverManager.getConnection().
  • Spring: BeanFactory / ApplicationContext.getBean() and @Bean methods are factories for objects.

Structure (text diagram)

 Client ---asks "sms"---> NotificationFactory
                               |  decides
                               v
                +-----------------------------+
                | Notification (interface)    |
                +-----------------------------+
                    ^             ^
                    |             |
               EmailNotification  SmsNotification

When to use

  • The exact class is known only at run time (user choice, config file, request parameter).
  • Object creation is complicated (many steps, defaults) and you want it in one place.
  • You want to add new product types without editing the client.

When NOT to use

  • There is only one concrete class and no likely second one - a plain new is simpler.
  • The factory would just forward to a constructor with no decision and no extra logic.
  • You end up with a giant if-else factory that is edited for every new type (use a registry instead).

Sample 1 - Notification factory

The client only knows the Notification interface and a text key. Adding "whatsapp" later means one new class and one new line in the factory; main does not change.

Sample 2 - Transport factory with the fare calculated inside the product

Here every product has behaviour (fare). The caller never needs to know which class computes it - this is the real benefit of returning an interface.

intermediate.content:
Design the factory method in which multiple objects are stored called as Factory Design Pattern.
• The Factory Design Pattern is a Creational Pattern that provides an interface for creating objects but allows subclasses or methods to decide which class to instantiate.
• It promotes loose coupling by removing the need to bind application-specific classes into code.

Key Points

• Encapsulates Object Creation → Centralized place for creating objects.
• Loose Coupling → Client code doesn’t know which class it gets, only the interface.
• Promotes Reusability & Flexibility → Easy to add new product types.
• Return Common Interface / Superclass → Factory method returns a parent type.
• Real-Life Example → IRCTC Website.

Advantages

• Centralized object creation.
• Reduces tight coupling.
• Makes code more maintainable & scalable.

Disadvantages

• Adds extra classes (slightly more complexity).
• Sometimes makes debugging harder due to indirect instantiation.

Why?

• Sometime our application or frameworks don’t know what kind of object has to create at run time.
It only knows when it has to create.
• Another issue is that class will contain object of another classes, this can be easily achieved by just using the new keyword and the class constructor. The problem with this approach is that it is very hard coded approach to create the object as this creates dependency between two classes.
To overcome this above situation, we should go for factory pattern.

When?

When user wants the specific object at run time.

Example

Suppose we have requirement to book AC ticket for First tier, second tier and Third tier. Follow these steps:

  1. Step 1: Create the interface Booking.
  2. Step 2: Create the concrete class First tier, which implements the same interface.
  3. Step 3: Create the concrete class Second tier, which implements the same interface.
  4. Step 4: Create the concrete class Third tier, which implements the same interface.
  5. Step 5: Create class BookingFactory to generate the object of the concrete class.
  6. Step 6: Create the client class that gets the object from the factory by passing the data.
Step 1: Create the interface Booking.
Step 2: Create the concrete class First tier, which implements the same interface.
Step 3: Create the concrete class Second tier, which implements the same interface.
Step 4: Create the concrete class Third tier, which implements the same interface.
Step 5: Create class BookingFactory to generate the object of the concrete class. The factory method takes the input first, second or third and returns the matching object.
Step 6: Use the factory class to get the object of the concrete class by passing the data.

Variant 1 - Parameterised factory using an enum

What it shows: the factory takes an enum instead of a String. Why: a typo like "smss" becomes a compile error, and a switch over an enum can be checked by the compiler for missing cases.

Variant 2 - Factory with a Map registry of Suppliers

What it shows: instead of an if-else chain, a Map<String, Supplier> stores how to build each type. Why: the factory follows the Open/Closed Principle: new types register themselves, the factory code never changes.

Variant 3 - Static factory methods (Effective Java, Item 1)

What it shows: a class with a private constructor and named creation methods. Why: names such as of, zero, fromPaise explain intent, can return a cached object, and can validate input - things a constructor cannot do.

Variant 4 - The classic GoF Factory Method (subclass decides)

What it shows: an abstract creator with a createDocument() method that subclasses override, while shared logic stays in the base class. Why: the base class contains the workflow (open) and only the "which object" step varies - the Template Method idea combined with a factory.

Common mistakes and how to avoid them

  • Returning the concrete type: if the factory returns EmailNotification instead of Notification, clients are coupled again. Always return the interface.
  • Growing if-else chain: every new type edits the factory. Switch to a registry map or a ServiceLoader.
  • Returning null for unknown input: causes NullPointerException far from the cause. Throw IllegalArgumentException or return Optional.
  • Factory that also holds business logic: keep it to creation only.
  • Stringly-typed keys: prefer an enum to avoid typo bugs.

Factory Method vs Abstract Factory (comparison)

PointFactory (Method)Abstract Factory
CreatesOne product typeA family of related products
MechanismOne method, often overriddenAn interface with several create methods
Typical exampleNotification by channelButton + Checkbox for one theme
Adding a new product kindEasyHard (every factory changes)
Adding a new familyAdd a subclass or branchEasy (add one factory)

expert.content:
Problem in Simple Factory

Using multiple if-else blocks violates Open Closed Principle (OCP). Every new type requires modifying factory class.

Solution: Use Polymorphism (Factory Method Pattern)

Factory Using Enum (Cleaner Approach)

Removes if-else and improves readability.

Factory Pattern in Frameworks

  • Spring → BeanFactory
  • Hibernate → SessionFactory
  • Java → Calendar.getInstance()
  • JDBC → DriverManager.getConnection()

When NOT to Use Factory?

  • When object creation is simple
  • When only one implementation exists

Factory vs Abstract Factory

  • Factory → Creates one product
  • Abstract Factory → Creates families of related products

Factory Pattern with Dependency Injection (Spring Example)

Modern applications rarely use manual factories. Instead, frameworks like Spring internally use Factory pattern with Dependency Injection.

How Spring Uses Factory?

  • BeanFactory
  • ApplicationContext
  • @Bean annotated methods

Spring container decides which object to create at runtime. Client only depends on interface.

Factory with Reflection (Dynamic Object Creation)

Instead of using if-else or switch, we can dynamically create objects using Reflection. This makes factory fully dynamic.

⚠️ Used in Frameworks & Libraries

Factory with Registry Pattern

Instead of modifying factory every time, we can register objects in Map. This follows Open Closed Principle properly.

Best for Scalable Systems

Thread-Safe Factory

If factory manages shared resources, it must be thread-safe.

Example:

Factory Pattern + SOLID Principles

How Factory Supports SOLID:

  • S - Single Responsibility → Object creation separated
  • O - Open Closed → Add new product without modifying client
  • L - Liskov Substitution → Subtypes replace parent type
  • D - Dependency Inversion → Depend on abstraction

Common Mistakes

  • Putting business logic inside factory
  • Using too many if-else blocks
  • Violating OCP
  • Creating God Factory class

Real Industry Use Cases

  • JDBC DriverManager → Returns driver implementation
  • Calendar.getInstance()
  • LoggerFactory in SLF4J
  • Spring BeanFactory
  • Hibernate SessionFactory
  • Microservices → Strategy selection based on config

Performance Consideration

  • Factory adds slight abstraction overhead
  • Reflection-based factory is slower
  • Best approach → Registry or Dependency Injection

Factory vs Factory Method vs Abstract Factory

Type Creates Complexity
Simple Factory One type of object Low
Factory Method Delegates creation to subclasses Medium
Abstract Factory Family of related objects High

Factory Method is a step towards Abstract Factory.

Real-time example 1 - Payment gateway selection

An e-commerce app supports several gateways. The checkout code asks a factory for a gateway based on the customer's choice and never mentions Razorpay or PayPal. Unknown gateways are rejected with a clear error.

Real-time example 2 - Report exporter chosen by file extension

The same data is exported to CSV or JSON depending on the requested file name. The factory inspects the extension, so the reporting module stays closed for modification when a new format (for example XML) is added.

Sample mini project - Tour package builder service

A small booking engine: a PackageFactory creates TourPackage objects for a destination type, a BookingService prices them with a group discount, and main prints a readable summary. Each class has one clear job.

Thread-safety, testing and Spring notes

  • Thread-safety: a factory with no mutable state is automatically thread-safe. If you use a registry map that is filled at start-up and then read-only, use Map.of or ConcurrentHashMap.
  • Testing: test the factory with one assertion per key (returns the right type, throws for unknown). Because clients depend on the interface, they are tested with a fake product.
  • Spring: inject Map<String, PaymentGateway> and Spring fills it with all beans keyed by bean name - a ready-made registry factory. @Bean methods and FactoryBean<T> are the container's own factories; ObjectProvider<T> creates prototype beans on demand.
  • ServiceLoader: java.util.ServiceLoader discovers implementations from the classpath so even the registry needs no manual registration.

Anti-patterns

  • Switch-statement factory growing forever: every release edits the same class. Use registration.
  • Factory plus Singleton plus static state: hidden global state makes tests order-dependent.
  • Over-engineering: a factory in front of a single class with no variation is just noise.
  • Reflection with Class.forName on user input: a security hole; map known keys to known classes instead.

interviewQA: What problem does the Factory pattern solve?

It removes the direct use of new ConcreteClass() from client code. The client asks for a product by a key or through an interface; creation logic lives in one place, so adding types does not change the client.
Simple Factory vs Factory Method vs Abstract Factory?

Simple Factory is one class with a static method that decides. Factory Method defers the decision to subclasses by overriding a creation method. Abstract Factory is an interface that creates a whole family of related products.
Why are static factory methods often better than constructors?
They have names, can return cached or subtype instances, can return null-safe results or Optionals, and hide the concrete class. Examples: List.of, Integer.valueOf, LocalDate.of.
How do you avoid the growing if-else in a factory?
Use a registry: Map from key to Supplier (or Function). Types register themselves at start-up, so the factory stays unchanged. In Spring, inject a Map of beans; in plain Java use ServiceLoader.
Does the factory pattern violate the Open/Closed Principle?
A switch-based factory does, because it is edited for every new type. A registry-based or subclass-based (Factory Method) design keeps it closed for modification and open for extension.
What should a factory return for an unknown key?
Throw IllegalArgumentException (fail fast) or return Optional. Returning null spreads NullPointerExceptions into callers.
How is a Spring BeanFactory related to this pattern?

BeanFactory/ApplicationContext is a factory that builds, wires and returns objects by name or type. Dependency injection is the more powerful modern replacement for hand-written factories in many cases.

topics.name: Abstract Factory Pattern

beginner.content:
Abstract Factory Pattern provides an interface for creating families of related objects without specifying their concrete classes - it's essentially a "factory of factories".

Real-Life Example:

  • A cross-platform UI toolkit that produces matching Button + Checkbox + ScrollBar for Windows OR macOS
  • A vehicle factory producing matching Engine + Tyres + Body for a Car OR a Bike

Why do we need Abstract Factory?

  • To ensure a group of related products are used together consistently (you never accidentally mix a Windows Button with a Mac Checkbox)
  • To keep client code independent of concrete product classes
  • To make swapping an entire "family" of products a one-line change

Factory Method vs Abstract Factory:

  • Factory Method creates ONE product via a single overridable method
  • Abstract Factory creates a FAMILY of related products via multiple methods on one factory interface

In one minute

An Abstract Factory is a "factory of factories": one interface with several create methods, each making one part of a product family. You choose one concrete factory (for example the Dark theme) and everything it builds - button, menu, checkbox - matches. The client code talks only to the abstract interfaces, so switching the whole family is a one-line change.

Real-life analogies

  • A furniture showroom with styles: choose "Modern" and you get a modern sofa, table and chair that look right together; choose "Classic" and the whole set changes.
  • A car company's plant: the "SUV line" makes SUV engine, SUV tyres and SUV body; the "Hatchback line" makes the matching hatchback parts.
  • A thali: pick "South Indian" and every item (rice, sambar, chutney) belongs to that cuisine; pick "Punjabi" and they all change together.

Where you see it in Java, the JDK and Spring

  • javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilderFactory and TransformerFactory produce a consistent family of XML tools for one implementation.
  • JDBC: a Connection creates matching Statement, PreparedStatement and ResultSet objects for one database vendor.
  • java.awt.Toolkit and Swing's LookAndFeel create a family of widgets for one look.
  • Spring: profile-specific configuration classes (@Profile("mysql") vs @Profile("postgres")) each provide a matching set of beans.

Structure (text diagram)

        Client
          |  uses only abstractions
          v
  +------------------+        +-----------+   +-----------+
  | GUIFactory       |------> | Button    |   | Menu      |
  | createButton()   |        +-----------+   +-----------+
  | createMenu()     |           ^     ^        ^     ^
  +------------------+           |     |        |     |
     ^            ^         LightBtn DarkBtn LightMenu DarkMenu
     |            |
 LightFactory  DarkFactory   (each builds ONE matching family)

When to use

  • Your code must work with several families of related products and keep them consistent.
  • You want to swap a whole platform, theme, vendor or region at once.
  • You want to hide the concrete product classes from the client.

When NOT to use

  • You have only one product type (a plain Factory Method is enough).
  • There is only one family and no plan for another.
  • New kinds of products are added often: every factory interface and implementation must change.

Sample 1 - Light and Dark theme families

The Screen class receives a ThemeFactory and builds a button and a label from it. Because both come from the same factory, they can never be from different themes.

Sample 2 - Regional meal combos

Each cuisine factory builds a matching main dish and drink. The caller prints a combo without knowing a single concrete class.

intermediate.content:
Variant 1 - Database vendor families

What it shows: a factory per database vendor creating a matching Connection and QueryBuilder. Why: MySQL uses LIMIT while Oracle uses FETCH FIRST; the pairing must stay consistent, and the application code should not care.

Variant 2 - Regional tax and currency family

What it shows: a factory per country creating a tax calculator and a currency formatter. Why: mixing Indian tax rules with a US currency format would be a bug; one factory per region makes that impossible. The invoice service is completely region-agnostic.

Variant 3 - Choosing the factory at run time from configuration

What it shows: the only place that names concrete factories is one small selector method; everything else uses the interface. Why: this is how real applications switch families based on a config value or environment, with no recompilation of the client.

Variant 4 - Factory of factories (FactoryProducer)

What it shows: one more level: a producer that hands out the right Abstract Factory by a category key. Why: when you have several independent families (shapes and colours here), clients ask one entry point for the factory they need.

Common mistakes and how to avoid them

  • Using one factory for unrelated products: an Abstract Factory is for families that must be used together. Otherwise use separate Factory Methods.
  • Leaking concrete types: if the client casts to DarkButton the benefit is lost. Keep the client on the interfaces.
  • Mixing factories in one object: do not create a button from the light factory and a label from the dark one. Inject one factory and use only it.
  • Interface explosion: adding a new product kind (a Slider) means editing the factory interface and every implementation. Plan the product list before choosing this pattern.
  • Hard-coding new DarkThemeFactory() in many places: create it once at the composition root (or in a config selector) and pass it down.

Abstract Factory vs Factory Method (comparison)

PointAbstract FactoryFactory Method
ScopeFamily of related productsSingle product
Typical structureInterface with several create methodsOne overridable method
Extension: new variant (family)Add one factory classAdd one subclass
Extension: new product kindTouches every factoryNot applicable
Guarantees consistencyYes, by constructionNo
Often implemented withSeveral Factory Methods inside one classTemplate Method

expert.content:
Real-time example 1 - Repository layer for two databases

A service layer must run against MySQL in development and PostgreSQL in production. The factory returns a matching Repository and IdGenerator pair: MySQL uses auto-increment, PostgreSQL uses sequences. The business service is identical for both.

Real-time example 2 - Country-specific messaging kit

A notification service sends the same business event in each country's style: the language of the greeting and the preferred channel come as a matching pair from one factory. New countries are added by writing one more factory.

Sample mini project - Vehicle assembly line

Two assembly lines (Car and Bike) each produce a matching Engine, Tyre and Body. The AssemblyPlant builds and costs a vehicle without knowing which family it is working with; a final report prints one readable summary per vehicle.

Thread-safety, testing and Spring notes

  • Thread-safety: stateless factories are safe to share, so keep them immutable and make them singletons (or Spring singleton beans). Products can be per-call objects.
  • Testing: write a FakeFactory that returns stub products and pass it to the client; no real database or network is needed. Also write one test per concrete factory that asserts all products belong to the same family.
  • Spring: use @Profile or @ConditionalOnProperty so exactly one configuration class (the family) is active, each declaring its matching @Bean methods. Spring Boot's auto-configuration is essentially an abstract factory chosen by classpath and properties.
  • Dependency injection vs Abstract Factory: with a DI container you often do not write the factory at all - you swap a whole module of beans. Keep the explicit pattern for plain Java or when the family is chosen at run time.

Anti-patterns

  • Fat factory interface: 15 create methods that no single client needs. Split by cohesion.
  • Static global factory: Factories.current mutated at run time creates mixed families and test pollution.
  • Instanceof checks on products: a sign the abstraction is wrong.
  • Premature abstraction: building three layers for a family that will never get a second member.

interviewQA: What is the Abstract Factory pattern?

A creational pattern that gives an interface for creating families of related objects without naming their concrete classes. The client picks a concrete factory once and every product it creates belongs to the same family.
How does Abstract Factory differ from Factory Method?

Factory Method creates a single product through one overridable method. Abstract Factory groups several factory methods in one interface to create a whole family. Abstract Factory is often implemented using Factory Methods.
What is the main drawback of Abstract Factory?
Adding a new product kind forces changes to the abstract factory interface and every concrete factory. Adding a new family is easy; adding a new kind of product is hard.
Give a real JDK example.
DocumentBuilderFactory and TransformerFactory in JAXP; JDBC Connection producing matching Statement and ResultSet; Swing LookAndFeel producing a consistent set of widgets.
How does it support the Open/Closed and Dependency Inversion principles?
The client depends only on abstractions (DIP), and new families are added as new classes without editing the client (OCP).
How would you test code that uses an Abstract Factory?
Inject a fake factory returning stub or mock products, and add tests per concrete factory verifying that it creates the expected, mutually consistent products.
What is a factory of factories?
A FactoryProducer (or similar) that returns the correct Abstract Factory for a given key, so clients have a single entry point to obtain factories.
How do Spring profiles relate to this pattern?
A profile activates one configuration class whose @Bean methods supply a consistent set of beans, which acts like selecting a concrete factory for a whole family.

topics.name: Builder Pattern

beginner.content:
Builder Pattern constructs a complex object step by step, separating the construction process from the final representation - avoiding constructors with a huge number of parameters ("telescoping constructors").

Real-Life Example:

  • Building a House (foundation, walls, roof, paint - each step optional/configurable)
  • Building a Meal order (burger, with/without cheese, with/without fries, drink size)
  • Java's own StringBuilder and StringBuffer

Why do we need Builder?

  • To avoid constructors with 6, 8, 10+ parameters that are impossible to read at the call site
  • To make optional parameters truly optional, instead of forcing null placeholders
  • To make the object immutable once built
  • To read fluently: new Pizza.Builder().size(12).cheese(true).build()

In one minute

A Builder constructs a complex object step by step. Instead of one constructor with ten confusing parameters, you call readable methods (.size("large").extraCheese()) and finish with .build(). It solves the telescoping constructor problem, lets you skip optional values, and can produce an immutable object that is checked once, at the end.

Real-life analogies

  • Ordering a sandwich at a counter: bread, filling, sauce, extras - you add each choice in turn and the sandwich is made at the end.
  • Building a house: foundation, walls, roof, paint in a fixed order, by a builder following your plan.
  • Filling a railway reservation form: name, age, train, class, berth preference - many fields, some optional, one submit button.

Where you see it in Java, the JDK and Spring

  • StringBuilder and StringBuffer (append step by step, then toString()).
  • java.util.stream.Stream.Builder, Locale.Builder, java.net.http.HttpRequest.newBuilder(), ProcessBuilder.
  • Calendar.Builder and DateTimeFormatterBuilder.
  • Spring: UriComponentsBuilder, BeanDefinitionBuilder, RestClient.builder(), Spring Security's http.authorizeHttpRequests(...) chain; Lombok generates builders with @Builder.

Structure (text diagram)

 Client
   |  Laptop.builder().cpu("i7").ram(16).ssd(512).build()
   v
+----------------------+   build()   +-----------------+
| Laptop.Builder       |-----------> | Laptop          |
| - cpu, ram, ssd...   |             | (immutable)     |
| + cpu(..) : Builder  |             | - cpu, ram, ... |
| + ram(..) : Builder  |             +-----------------+
| + build() : Laptop   |
+----------------------+
 each setter returns "this" so calls can be chained

When to use

  • A class has many fields and several are optional.
  • You want an immutable object but still want readable creation code.
  • Construction needs validation across several fields or several steps.

When NOT to use

  • The class has two or three required fields - a simple constructor is clearer.
  • The object is mutable and short-lived; plain setters are enough.
  • You would write a builder by hand for each of dozens of classes without Lombok or records.

Sample 1 - The problem and the fix: laptop configuration

The first line shows how unreadable a long constructor call is (what is true? what is 512?). The builder version names every value.

Sample 2 - A burger order with default values

Unspecified options fall back to sensible defaults, so the simplest order is a one-liner and a complex one is still readable.

intermediate.content:
Variant 1 - Builder with validation in build()

What it shows: required fields and cross-field rules are checked in build(). Why: an object that exists is guaranteed valid, so the rest of the program never needs defensive checks. Errors are reported with clear messages instead of a half-built object.

Variant 2 - Record plus a hand-written builder (Lombok-style)

What it shows: a Java record gives an immutable value class for free, and a small nested builder adds named, optional parameters plus a toBuilder() copy. Why: this is what Lombok's @Builder generates; with records you need almost no boilerplate.

Variant 3 - Director controlling the build order

What it shows: the classic GoF form. A Director knows the recipe (which steps, in what order); different builders produce different representations from the same steps. Why: the same construction process can create an HTML page or a plain-text page.

Variant 4 - Step builder (compiler enforces required fields)

What it shows: each step returns a different interface, so build() only becomes available after all required values are given. Why: you move validation from run time to compile time; forgetting to() does not compile.

Variant 5 - Immutable object with a collection and defensive copying

What it shows: the builder collects repeated values (recipients) and the product stores an unmodifiable copy. Why: if you keep the builder's list, later calls on the builder - or on the exposed list - would silently change an "immutable" object.

Common mistakes and how to avoid them

  • Forgetting to return this: a setter that returns void breaks the chain. Every builder method must return the builder.
  • Validating in setters instead of build(): cross-field rules (check-out after check-in) can only be checked once all values are known.
  • Reusing a builder after build(): if the product shares the builder's list, later changes leak into it. Copy collections in the product constructor.
  • Making the product mutable anyway: public setters on the product defeat the purpose. Keep fields final.
  • Builder for everything: for two or three fields use a constructor or a record directly.

Builder vs Factory (comparison)

PointBuilderFactory
GoalAssemble one complex object in stepsChoose which class to instantiate
ResultUsually one class, many configurationsDifferent classes behind one interface
Client inputMany values, often optionalUsually a key or type
Creation callMany method calls then build()One method call
Typical exampleHttpRequest, StringBuilderCalendar.getInstance(), List.of()
Can combine?Yes - a factory can return a pre-configured builder.

expert.content:
Real-time example 1 - HTTP request builder

A tiny REST client model: method, URL, headers, query parameters and an optional JSON body. The builder produces an immutable request and validates that a body is only sent with POST or PUT. This mirrors java.net.http.HttpRequest.newBuilder().

Real-time example 2 - Report builder with sections and totals

A sales report is assembled from a title, any number of line items and an optional footer. The builder keeps the running total, so the finished report object is read-only and consistent.

Sample mini project - SQL query builder

A small fluent SQL builder with a Condition class, a Query product and a QueryBuilder. It validates that a table exists, supports several WHERE conditions, ordering and a limit, and prints the final SQL. Typical of libraries such as jOOQ or Hibernate Criteria.

Thread-safety, testing and Spring notes

  • Thread-safety: a builder is not thread-safe and should not be shared; create one per object. The built product, being immutable with final fields, is safely shareable between threads without locks.
  • Testing: test valid builds, each validation failure, defaults, and that changing the builder after build() does not change the product. For equality in tests, give the product equals/hashCode (records do it for you).
  • Lombok: @Builder generates the nested builder; @Builder.Default sets defaults, toBuilder = true adds toBuilder(), and @Singular creates add-one methods for collections.
  • Spring: UriComponentsBuilder, MockMvcRequestBuilders, WebClient.builder() and RestClient.builder() are everyday builders. Configuration objects built with a builder can be exposed as a @Bean so the finished immutable object is injected, not the builder.
  • Jackson: annotate with @JsonDeserialize(builder = ...) to deserialize JSON into an immutable object through its builder.

Anti-patterns

  • Builder that returns a different mutable object each time but exposes setters on the product.
  • Telescoping builders: a builder with forty methods signals the class itself is too large; split it.
  • Skipping validation so that build() returns objects in illegal states.
  • Shared static builder: reusing one builder instance across threads or requests leaks state.

interviewQA: What problem does the Builder pattern solve?

The telescoping constructor and the JavaBean inconsistency problems: objects with many optional parameters. A builder sets values by name step by step, validates once, and returns a complete (often immutable) object.
How is Builder different from Factory?
A factory decides which class to create and usually takes one key; a builder assembles one complex object from many steps. Factory returns the product at once, Builder returns it after build().
What is the role of the Director in the GoF Builder?

The Director encapsulates the construction sequence and calls the builder steps in the right order, so the same process can create different representations with different builders. Modern fluent builders often omit it.
Why make the product immutable and copy collections?
So that once built, no one can alter its state: no setters, final fields, and defensive copies (or unmodifiable lists) prevent changes through retained references to the builder or exposed lists.
Where should validation go: setters or build()?
In build(). Only then are all values present, so cross-field rules (end after start) can be checked and an invalid object can never be created.
How does Lombok @Builder relate to the pattern?
It generates the nested builder class, fluent methods and build() at compile time; @Builder.Default, @Singular and toBuilder refine it. It removes boilerplate but the pattern is the same.
Name Builders in the JDK.
StringBuilder, HttpRequest.newBuilder(), ProcessBuilder, Stream.builder(), Locale.Builder and DateTimeFormatterBuilder.
Is a builder thread-safe?
Normally no. Use one builder per thread/object; the built immutable product is the thing you share.

topics.name: Prototype Pattern

beginner.content:
Prototype Pattern creates new objects by copying (cloning) an existing object instead of building it from scratch - useful when object creation is expensive (heavy DB call, complex computation) but a near-identical copy is cheap.

Real-Life Example:

  • Photocopying a document instead of retyping it
  • Cloning a fully-configured game character/enemy template to spawn new instances
  • Java's own Object.clone() and the Cloneable interface

Why do we need Prototype?

  • To avoid re-running expensive initialization logic for every new object
  • To create objects without depending on their concrete class (works via an interface reference)
  • To easily produce variations of a "base" configured object

Shallow vs Deep Clone:

  • Shallow clone copies primitive fields directly but COPIES THE REFERENCE for object fields - both the original and the clone point to the SAME nested object
  • Deep clone recursively clones nested objects too, so the clone is fully independent

In one minute

The Prototype pattern creates a new object by copying an existing one (the prototype) instead of building it from scratch with new. It is useful when creating an object is costly (loading data, many settings) or when you want many similar objects that differ only slightly. The key question is always: is the copy shallow (shares inner objects) or deep (copies everything)?

Real-life analogies

  • Photocopying a filled form: you copy it once and change only the name and date, rather than rewriting every field.
  • A cell dividing: the new cell starts as a copy of the original.
  • A template Excel file: "Save As" a new file, then edit what differs.

Where you see it in Java, the JDK and Spring

  • Object.clone() with the Cloneable marker interface; arrays have clone() too.
  • Copy constructors in collections: new ArrayList<>(other), new HashMap<>(map), plus List.copyOf(...).
  • Arrays.copyOf, and Date.clone().
  • Spring: beans with @Scope("prototype") give a new instance on every request (the container creates a fresh one from the definition); BeanUtils.copyProperties copies state between objects.

Structure (text diagram)

+--------------------+         +----------------------+
| Prototype          |         | Client               |
| + copy() : Prototype| <------ | p2 = p1.copy();      |
+--------------------+         | p2.setName("new");   |
        ^                       +----------------------+
        |
+--------------------+   copy() builds a new object with the
| ConcretePrototype  |   same field values as "this"
| - fields           |
+--------------------+

When to use

  • Object creation is expensive (database load, parsing, heavy computation) and a copy is cheaper.
  • You need many objects that are almost the same (game enemies, document templates, test data).
  • You want to avoid a parallel hierarchy of factories for each class.

When NOT to use

  • The object is trivial to construct - a normal constructor is simpler.
  • The object contains resources that cannot be copied (open files, sockets, threads).
  • Object graphs contain cycles or complex shared references that make deep copies error-prone.

Sample 1 - Copying an invoice template with a copy method

Instead of the awkward Cloneable, this uses a plain copy() method in the class. The template stays untouched; each invoice is a copy with only customer and amount changed.

Sample 2 - Game enemies cloned from a prototype

A "Soldier" with an expensive set-up (here simulated by a message) is created once. Reinforcements are cheap copies; only position differs.

intermediate.content:
Variant 1 - Shallow copy versus deep copy with Cloneable

What it shows: super.clone() copies field values, so an inner object (the address) is shared between original and clone. Changing it through the clone changes the original too. Why it matters: this is the number-one prototype bug. The second class overrides clone() to copy the inner object as well.

Variant 2 - Copy constructor (the recommended alternative to clone)

What it shows: a constructor that takes an object of the same type and copies it, including a deep copy of the list. Why: no Cloneable, no checked exception, no casts, works with final fields, and the intent is obvious.

Variant 3 - Prototype registry (cache of ready-made prototypes)

What it shows: a registry that holds named prototypes and hands out copies. Why: clients ask for "student-template" by name and get a fresh independent copy each time, without knowing the class or how it was made.

Variant 4 - Deep copy through serialization

What it shows: writing an object graph to bytes and reading it back produces a complete deep copy, however deeply nested. Why: it saves writing copy code for large graphs. Cost: every class must implement Serializable, and it is slower than manual copying.

Variant 5 - Copying collections and arrays correctly

What it shows: the everyday "prototype" operations of the JDK and their depth: clone() on an array, new ArrayList<>(list), and List.copyOf. All are shallow: the container is copied, the elements are shared. Why: you must know this before trusting a "copy" of a list of mutable objects.

Common mistakes and how to avoid them

  • Shallow copy surprises: mutable fields (lists, dates, other objects) must be copied in the copy method. Test by changing the copy and checking the original.
  • Forgetting implements Cloneable: super.clone() then throws CloneNotSupportedException.
  • Returning the registry's prototype itself: the caller changes it and corrupts the template. Always return a copy.
  • clone() with final fields or inheritance: clone cannot reassign final fields and subclasses can forget to override it. Prefer copy constructors or a copy() method.
  • Copying resources: do not clone sockets, streams or threads; re-open them in the copy.
  • Cyclic references in deep copy: a naive recursive copy loops forever. Serialization handles cycles; hand-written code needs an identity map.

Prototype vs Factory (comparison)

PointPrototypeFactory
How objects are madeCopied from an existing instanceConstructed with new in the factory
Knowledge neededA ready prototype objectThe concrete class
State of new objectStarts with the prototype's current stateStarts with default state
Best whenCreation is costly or configuration-heavyClass choice varies at run time
Main riskShallow versus deep copy bugsGrowing switch statements
Can combine?Yes - a factory can keep prototypes and return copies (a prototype registry).

expert.content:
Real-time example 1 - Offer-letter template system

HR keeps an offer-letter template containing fixed clauses and a benefits list. Each candidate gets a deep copy; personal fields and an extra benefit are added to the copy only. The template is never modified, which is exactly why Prototype is used for document generation.

Real-time example 2 - Game character spawner with prototype registry

A level loads a few prototype monsters once (the costly step) and spawns hundreds of copies. Using a registry means the spawner works with names from a level file and needs no knowledge of the monster classes. Each copy has its own position and health so damage to one does not affect another.

Sample mini project - Exam paper generator

A teacher defines a master question paper (the prototype) once. For each student the system makes a deep copy, stamps the roll number, shuffles nothing but changes the paper code, and prints a readable summary. The master is verified to be untouched at the end - the point of Prototype.

Thread-safety, testing and Spring notes

  • Thread-safety: a prototype that is only read while copying is safe to share. If threads can modify it, make the copy() method synchronized or keep the prototype immutable and copy-on-write. Never hand out the prototype itself.
  • Testing: assert four things - the copy equals the original (or has the same values), the copy is not the same reference, mutating the copy leaves the original unchanged, and nested objects are different references (deep copy proof).
  • Spring: a bean with @Scope("prototype") is created anew on every getBean or injection point (a singleton bean that needs a fresh prototype each time should use ObjectProvider or @Lookup). Singleton beans are shared; prototype beans' destroy callbacks are not called by the container.
  • Mapping libraries: BeanUtils.copyProperties and MapStruct perform shallow property copies between objects; check nested objects yourself.
  • Records and immutability: immutable objects need no defensive copy of themselves; "copy with a change" is done with a wither or toBuilder().

Anti-patterns

  • Relying on Object.clone() for new code: it is widely regarded as broken design (no constructor call, checked exception, final-field problems).
  • Deep copy by hand everywhere: duplicate copy code that drifts out of date when a field is added; centralise it or use serialization/mapping carefully.
  • Mutable shared prototype: any client changing a global template silently changes every future copy.
  • Cloning to avoid understanding construction: if copies need major changes, a Builder or Factory is clearer.

interviewQA: What is the Prototype pattern and when is it useful?

It creates new objects by copying an existing instance instead of using new. It is useful when construction is expensive, when many similar objects are needed, or when the exact class is unknown to the client.
Shallow copy vs deep copy?

A shallow copy duplicates the object but shares its referenced inner objects; a deep copy duplicates the inner objects too. With a shallow copy, mutating a nested object through the clone also changes the original.
Why is Object.clone() considered problematic?

It bypasses constructors, needs the Cloneable marker, throws a checked exception, does a shallow copy by default, conflicts with final fields and is easy to get wrong in subclasses. Copy constructors or copy methods are preferred.
How can you create a deep copy in Java?
Override clone() and copy mutable fields, use a copy constructor, serialize and deserialize the object, or use a mapping library; in each case verify that nested objects are different references.
What is a Prototype registry?
A map of named prototypes. Clients ask for a name and receive a fresh copy, so they do not depend on concrete classes and expensive prototypes are built only once.
How does Prototype relate to Spring bean scopes?
The prototype scope makes the container return a new bean instance on every request, which is the same intent. Singleton beans are shared; prototype beans are not cached or managed after creation.
Does Arrays.copyOf or new ArrayList(list) give a deep copy?
No. They create a new container but share the element references, so mutable elements are shared. Copy the elements yourself if you need independence.

topics.name: Adapter Pattern

beginner.content:
Adapter Pattern lets two incompatible interfaces work together by wrapping one of them in an object (the adapter) that translates calls between them.

Real-Life Example:

  • A travel plug adapter that lets a US plug fit into an Indian socket
  • A memory card reader that lets an SD card connect to a USB port
  • Java's own Arrays.asList() adapting an array to the List interface

Why do we need Adapter?

  • To reuse existing/legacy code that has an incompatible interface, without modifying it
  • To let two independently-developed classes collaborate
  • To integrate a third-party library's class into your own interface

In one minute

An Adapter sits between a client that expects interface A and a class that offers interface B. The client calls A; the adapter translates the call into B. Neither side changes. Think "converter", not "new feature".

Everyday analogies

  • Travel plug adapter: your charger stays the same, the wall socket stays the same, the adapter sits between them.
  • Card reader: a microSD card cannot talk to a USB port, the reader converts the signals.
  • Human translator: a Hindi speaker and a Tamil speaker both stay as they are; the translator maps sentences one way and the other.

Where you see it in Java / JDK / Spring

  • java.io.InputStreamReader adapts a byte InputStream to the character Reader interface.
  • java.util.Arrays.asList(...) adapts an array to List.
  • java.util.Collections.enumeration(...) and Enumeration.asIterator() convert between old and new iteration APIs.
  • Executors.callable(Runnable) adapts a Runnable to a Callable.
  • Spring MVC's HandlerAdapter lets DispatcherServlet call very different controller styles through one interface.

Structure (object adapter)

Client ---> Target (interface)
                ^
                |  implements
             Adapter ---has-a---> Adaptee (incompatible class)

When to use / when NOT to use

  • Use it when you must reuse a class whose source you cannot (or should not) change: legacy code, a third-party SDK, generated code.
  • Use it when several vendors expose similar features with different method names.
  • Do NOT use it when you own both sides: just rename the method or change the interface.
  • Do NOT use it to add behaviour (that is Decorator) or to simplify many classes (that is Facade).

Sample: a Fahrenheit sensor behind a Celsius interface

The weather station code only understands Celsius. A purchased sensor reports Fahrenheit. The adapter converts, so no existing code changes.

intermediate.content:
Sample 1: object adapter (composition)

What it shows: the adapter holds the legacy object as a field and delegates to it. Why: this is the default choice, because it works with any subclass of the adaptee and is easy to swap or mock.

Sample 2: class adapter (inheritance)

What it shows: the adapter extends the adaptee and implements the target. Why: it can reach protected members and avoids one extra object, but it locks you to one concrete adaptee and needs a language that allows it (in Java the target must be an interface).

Sample 3: a JDK-style adapter, Enumeration to Iterator

What it shows: adapting the legacy Enumeration (Vector, Hashtable era) to the modern Iterator. Why: new code can use for-each and streams with old APIs. The JDK does the same in Collections.list and Enumeration.asIterator().

Common mistakes

  • Fat adapter: putting business rules in it. An adapter only translates names, units and formats.
  • Leaking the adaptee type through the target interface, so clients still depend on the vendor class.
  • Swallowing exceptions during translation; map them to your own exception type instead.
  • Creating an adapter when you own the code and could simply refactor.
  • Forgetting round-trip loss, e.g. converting double to int silently drops precision.

Adapter vs Facade vs Proxy vs Decorator

PatternInterface of the wrapperIntentWraps
AdapterDifferent from the wrapped oneMake incompatible APIs fitUsually one object
DecoratorSame as the wrapped oneAdd behaviourOne object, stackable
ProxySame as the wrapped oneControl access (lazy, cache, security)One object
FacadeNew, simpler interfaceHide a complex subsystemMany objects

expert.content:
Real-time example 1: payment gateway adapter

The checkout talks to one PaymentProcessor interface. Each vendor has its own method names, amount units (rupees vs paise) and result codes. Adapters hide all that, so adding a vendor never touches checkout code.

Real-time example 2: logging adapter (the SLF4J idea)

Application code logs through its own AppLogger. The adapter plugs in java.util.logging, so the logging library can be swapped without touching business classes. This is exactly how SLF4J bindings and Spring's commons-logging bridge work.

Sample mini project: travel-booking aggregator

Three suppliers return fares in three shapes. One adapter per supplier converts them into a common Fare record; the aggregator then picks the cheapest. Run it and read the result table.

Testing, Spring and performance notes

  • Testing: depend on the target interface, then unit-test each adapter with a fake adaptee and assert on unit conversions and edge values (zero, negative, null).
  • Spring: register adapters as beans and inject them by interface, optionally as Map<String, PaymentProcessor> keyed by bean name to pick a vendor at runtime. HandlerAdapter, HttpMessageConverter and JpaVendorAdapter are framework examples.
  • Performance: an adapter adds one call; the cost is only in conversion (parsing, boxing). Avoid re-parsing on every call, convert once and cache.
  • Keep adapters in an anti-corruption layer package so vendor types never appear in your domain model.

Anti-patterns

  • Adapter chain: adapting an adapter of an adapter; refactor to one translation.
  • Two-way god adapter that implements five interfaces.
  • Using reflection-based generic adapters everywhere, which hides errors until runtime.

interviewQA: What problem does the Adapter pattern solve?

It lets a client use a class whose interface does not match what the client expects, by wrapping that class in an adapter that translates calls. The adaptee and the client stay unchanged, which supports the Open/Closed principle.
Class adapter vs object adapter?

A class adapter inherits from the adaptee and implements the target; an object adapter holds the adaptee as a field and delegates. Java prefers object adapters because they use composition, work with subclasses of the adaptee and are easier to test.
Give two Adapter examples in the JDK.
InputStreamReader (bytes to characters), Arrays.asList (array to List), Collections.enumeration and Enumeration.asIterator, Executors.callable (Runnable to Callable).
How is Adapter different from Facade?
Adapter changes the interface of one class to match an expected one. Facade defines a new, simpler interface over a whole subsystem of many classes.
How is Adapter different from Decorator and Proxy?
Decorator and Proxy keep the same interface as the wrapped object (adding behaviour or controlling access). Adapter deliberately exposes a different interface.
Where would you put adapters in a layered application?
At the boundary to external systems (an anti-corruption layer or infrastructure package), so domain code depends only on your own interfaces and vendor types never leak inward.

topics.name: Decorator Pattern

beginner.content:
Decorator Pattern attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically, by wrapping it in decorator objects - a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending behavior.

Real-Life Example:

  • Coffee shop: base Coffee, then wrap it with Milk, then Sugar, then Whipped Cream - each adds cost/description
  • Java's own BufferedReader(new FileReader(...)) and InputStreamReader chains

Why do we need Decorator?

  • To add behavior to individual objects at RUNTIME, without affecting other instances of the same class
  • To avoid an explosion of subclasses for every combination of features (e.g. MilkSugarCoffee, SugarCreamCoffee, ...)
  • To keep each responsibility in its own small class (Single Responsibility Principle)

In one minute

A Decorator wraps an object that has the same interface and adds behaviour before or after delegating to it. Because a decorator is itself a valid component, decorators can be stacked like layers of an onion, in any combination, at runtime. It replaces an explosion of subclasses such as SugarMilkCoffee, SugarCoffee, MilkCoffee.

Everyday analogies

  • Gift wrapping: the gift is the same, you add paper, then a ribbon, then a card.
  • Clothes: you add a shirt, a sweater, a jacket; each layer adds warmth without changing you.
  • Pizza toppings: base price plus each topping, chosen per order.

Where you see it in Java / JDK / Spring

  • java.io: BufferedInputStream, DataInputStream, GZIPOutputStream all wrap another stream (FilterInputStream is the abstract decorator).
  • Collections.unmodifiableList, synchronizedList, checkedList wrap a collection and tweak its behaviour.
  • HttpServletRequestWrapper and HttpServletResponseWrapper in the Servlet API.
  • Spring: BeanPostProcessor-created wrappers and ServerHttpRequestDecorator in WebFlux.

Structure

Component (interface)
   ^                  ^
   |                  |
ConcreteComponent   Decorator ---has-a---> Component
                       ^
              LoudDecorator, StampDecorator ...

client -> Stamp( Loud( Plain ) )   // each layer calls the next

When to use / when NOT to use

  • Use it to add optional features in many combinations without a subclass per combination.
  • Use it when responsibilities must be added or removed at runtime.
  • Do NOT use it when the order of wrapping is hard to reason about for your team, or when you need to remove a middle layer later.
  • Do NOT use it when the interface is huge: every decorator must forward every method.

Sample: message formatting layers

A plain message is wrapped by a trimming layer, a shouting layer and a stamp layer. Each layer is independent; changing the stack changes the result.

intermediate.content:
Sample 1: writing your own java.io decorator

What it shows: a FilterReader subclass that upper-cases every character, stacked with the JDK's BufferedReader. Why: this is how the real I/O library is designed; once you can write one filter you understand all of java.io.

Sample 2: pricing rules as decorators

What it shows: a base bill wrapped by discount, GST and delivery decorators. Why: every rule is tiny and testable on its own, and the shop can switch rules per customer by building a different stack.

Sample 3: wrapping order matters

What it shows: the same two decorators in two orders give different results. Why: a stack is a pipeline; compress-then-encrypt is valid, encrypt-then-compress is useless. Always document the intended order.

Sample 4: JDK collection decorators

What it shows: Collections.unmodifiableList and checkedList are decorators over a normal list. Why: you can hand out a read-only view of internal state without copying it, and the view still reflects later changes.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to forward a method in a decorator, so the wrapped behaviour silently disappears.
  • Relying on object identity or instanceof of the concrete component: a wrapped object is no longer that class.
  • Making decorators stateful and sharing one instance between stacks.
  • Allowing nonsensical orders (encrypt then compress) without documenting or enforcing the order, for example with a builder.
  • Using Decorator when the extra behaviour is a single fixed feature; a plain method is simpler.

Decorator vs similar patterns

PatternSame interface?PurposeTypical stacking
DecoratorYesAdd responsibilitiesMany layers, chosen by the client
ProxyYesControl access / lifecycleUsually one, often built by the proxy itself
AdapterNoConvert interfaceOne
CompositeYesTreat group like one objectMany children, not layers
Chain of ResponsibilityHandler chainOne handler may stop the chainEach link decides to pass on

expert.content:
Real-time example 1: request handler middleware

Web frameworks (servlet filters, Spring interceptors, Express middleware) are decorators in disguise. Here a flaky service is wrapped by retry, then by logging, without the service knowing. The retry layer is the interesting one: it re-calls the inner handler.

Real-time example 2: caching decorator over a repository

A slow repository (database) is wrapped by a caching decorator that implements the same interface. Callers do not change; hit and miss counts prove the cache works. This is the idea behind Spring's @Cacheable, although Spring builds the wrapper as a proxy.

Sample mini project: fort entry ticket with add-ons

A base ticket is wrapped by optional add-ons (guide, audio kit, parking). A small receipt printer walks the layers through lines() so each add-on shows up as its own line. Three visitors choose three different stacks.

Testing, Spring and performance notes

  • Testing: test each decorator against a mock or stub of the interface and verify it forwards exactly once (or the right number of times for retry). Test a few real stacks as integration tests, especially ordering.
  • Spring: @Transactional, @Cacheable and @Async are applied by wrapping your bean in a generated proxy that decorates it. Use @Primary or @Qualifier and a configuration class to assemble explicit decorator stacks of your own beans.
  • Performance: each layer adds a virtual call and maybe an allocation; fine for dozens of layers, but avoid creating a new stack per element in a hot loop. Buffering decorators (BufferedInputStream) are decorators that improve performance.
  • Prefer the builder or factory that returns the interface, so callers never see the concrete wrapping order.

Anti-patterns

  • Decorator soup: ten layers where nobody knows which one changed the result; log the stack in debug mode.
  • Leaky decorator: adding public methods that only exist on one decorator, forcing casts in clients.
  • Using inheritance for the same effect (MilkSugarCoffee) and creating a class explosion.

interviewQA: What is the Decorator pattern?
A structural pattern that adds responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in objects that share its interface. It is a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending behaviour.
Why is Decorator better than inheritance for optional features?
Inheritance fixes behaviour at compile time and needs a subclass per combination. Decorators are combined at runtime, so n features need n small classes instead of 2^n subclasses.
Name Decorator examples in the JDK.
BufferedInputStream, DataInputStream and GZIPOutputStream (FilterInputStream family), BufferedReader, Collections.unmodifiableList and synchronizedList, and the Servlet request and response wrappers.
Decorator vs Proxy: what is the difference?

Both implement the same interface and hold a reference to the real object. A decorator adds behaviour and is usually assembled by the client; a proxy controls access (lazy loading, security, remote call) and often manages the real object itself.
Does the order of decorators matter?

Yes. Each layer sees the result of the inner layers, so compress-then-encrypt differs from encrypt-then-compress, and a discount before tax differs from tax before discount. Document or encode the order in a builder.
What are the drawbacks of Decorator?
Many small classes, harder debugging through several layers, order sensitivity, and identity or instanceof checks no longer work on the wrapped component.

topics.name: Facade Pattern

beginner.content:
Facade Pattern provides a single, simplified interface in front of a complex subsystem made up of many interacting classes - the client talks only to the facade.

Real-Life Example:

  • A car's ignition button - one press ("start") hides fuel injection, spark plugs, starter motor, battery checks
  • A hotel "concierge" who coordinates room service, laundry, and cab booking behind one request

Why do we need Facade?

  • To hide the complexity of a subsystem with many classes behind one easy-to-use entry point
  • To reduce coupling between client code and a subsystem's internal classes
  • To provide a simpler, higher-level API without removing access to the underlying subsystem for advanced use cases

In one minute

A Facade is one easy class placed in front of a group of complicated classes (a subsystem). Clients call one or two simple methods such as checkout(); the facade calls the many subsystem classes in the right order. The subsystem is not hidden or locked: advanced users can still use it directly.

Everyday analogies

  • Hotel reception: you say "I want a room"; reception talks to housekeeping, billing and security for you.
  • Car ignition button: one press starts fuel pump, starter motor, ECU and dashboard.
  • Travel agent: one call books flight, hotel and cab.

Where you see it in Java / JDK / Spring

  • java.nio.file.Files: Files.readAllLines(path) hides channels, buffers, decoders and closing.
  • java.net.http.HttpClient hides sockets, TLS, redirects and threading behind send().
  • javax.faces.context.FacesContext, java.sql.DriverManager, and Executors (factory methods over thread pools).
  • Spring: JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate and JmsTemplate are facades over verbose low-level APIs; a @Service class is the facade of your business layer.
  • SLF4J's LoggerFactory is a facade over logging libraries.

Structure

Client ---> Facade ---> SubsystemA
                  ---> SubsystemB
                  ---> SubsystemC
(client may still use A, B, C directly if it needs fine control)

When to use / when NOT to use

  • Use it to give a simple entry point to a complex library or legacy system.
  • Use it to layer a system: one facade per layer reduces coupling between layers.
  • Do NOT use it to hide a badly designed subsystem forever; fix the design if you own it.
  • Do NOT let the facade become a god class that contains the business logic itself; it should only coordinate.

Sample: a good-night routine for a smart home

Three devices must be switched in a fixed order. The facade offers one method; the client does not know the order.

intermediate.content:
Sample 1: home theatre facade

What it shows: the textbook case, a facade starting and stopping five components in order. Why: the client avoids a dozen calls that must happen in exactly the right sequence, and the facade is the single place to change that sequence.

Sample 2: order checkout facade

What it shows: a facade returning a result object while hiding four services (inventory, payment, shipping, notification). Why: the web controller needs one call and one result; the rules about order, and what happens when one step refuses, live in one place.

Sample 3: a facade inside the JDK, java.nio.file.Files

What it shows: a write, read and delete round trip with three one-line calls. Why: the old way needs streams, writers, buffers and finally blocks; Files is a facade over all of that, which is exactly the benefit you want from your own facades.

Common mistakes

  • God facade: it grows to hundreds of methods and holds business rules. Split into several facades by use case.
  • Forcing every access through the facade and removing power-user access to the subsystem.
  • Making subsystem classes depend on the facade (a cycle). The dependency goes one way: facade to subsystem.
  • Returning subsystem types from the facade, so clients are coupled to them after all.
  • Swallowing errors: the facade should translate subsystem failures into meaningful exceptions or result objects.

Facade vs Adapter vs Mediator vs Proxy

PatternGoalDirection of knowledgeNumber of objects behind it
FacadeSimplify use of a subsystemFacade knows subsystem; subsystem does not know facadeMany
AdapterConvert one interface to anotherAdapter knows adapteeUsually one
MediatorLet peers talk without knowing each otherPeers know the mediatorMany peers
ProxyControl access, same interfaceProxy knows real subjectOne

expert.content:
Real-time example 1: trip planner as an aggregating facade (API gateway / BFF)

A mobile app needs weather, hotel price and cab estimate on one screen. The facade calls the three services in parallel with CompletableFuture and returns one combined answer, so the app makes a single request. This is the backend-for-frontend and API gateway idea at class level.

Real-time example 2: transactional facade with compensation

A facade that calls several services must decide what happens when step 3 fails. Here the booking facade releases the seat if payment fails (a tiny saga). In Spring the same job is done by a @Transactional service method; across services you need compensating actions as shown.

Sample mini project: hotel front desk

Guests only talk to FrontDesk. Behind it, rooms, billing and key cards cooperate. Check-in assigns a room and issues a key; check-out totals the nights and frees the room.

Testing, Spring and performance notes

  • Testing: inject the subsystem collaborators through the constructor so a unit test can pass mocks and verify call order with Mockito's InOrder. Keep one integration test with the real subsystem.
  • Spring: a @Service facade with constructor-injected beans is the standard way to expose a use case to controllers; put @Transactional on the facade method so all steps share one transaction. In microservices, an API gateway or BFF plays the same role over the network.
  • Performance: a facade is a convenient place to batch calls, run independent calls in parallel (as in the trip planner) and add caching or timeouts. Do not hide an N+1 call pattern behind a friendly method name.
  • Keep facades thin and stateless so they scale and are thread safe.

Anti-patterns

  • Facade as dumping ground: unrelated methods collected in one ApplicationManager.
