  • Pass-through facade that just renames subsystem methods; it adds a class and no simplification.
  • Chatty facade returning internal entities to remote clients, forcing many follow-up calls.

interviewQA: What is the Facade pattern?

A structural pattern that provides a single, simplified interface to a set of classes in a subsystem. It makes the subsystem easier to use and reduces coupling between clients and the subsystem internals.
Does a Facade hide the subsystem completely?
No. It offers a convenient path for common tasks, but the subsystem classes remain accessible for clients that need full control. Hiding is optional and is not the main point.
Give examples of Facade in the JDK and Spring.
java.nio.file.Files, HttpClient, Executors; in Spring JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate, JmsTemplate, and service-layer classes that coordinate repositories.
Facade vs Adapter?

Adapter converts one interface into another that a client expects, usually wrapping one class. Facade defines a new simpler interface over many classes. Adapter is about compatibility, Facade about simplicity.
How do you avoid a God-object facade?
Create several facades, each for one use case or module, keep them free of business rules (delegate to the subsystem), and keep dependencies one-directional.
How does Facade relate to microservices?
An API gateway or backend-for-frontend is a facade at service level: it aggregates calls to several services into one client-friendly endpoint, and can add authentication, caching and rate limiting.

topics.name: Proxy Pattern

beginner.content:
Proxy Pattern provides a placeholder/surrogate object that controls access to another (often expensive or remote) object - the proxy implements the same interface, so the client can't tell the difference.

Real-Life Example:

  • A credit card is a proxy for your bank account - it controls and checks access before money moves
  • A security guard checking ID before letting someone into a building (access control proxy)
  • Lazy-loading a huge image - a lightweight proxy stands in until the real image is actually needed

Why do we need Proxy?

  • Lazy initialization (Virtual Proxy): delay creating an expensive object until it's actually used
  • Access control (Protection Proxy): check permissions before delegating to the real object
  • Logging/Caching: add cross-cutting behavior around calls without changing the real object

In one minute

A Proxy is a stand-in object with the same interface as the real object (the real subject). Callers talk to the proxy; the proxy decides whether, when and how to forward the call. That gives you a place to add laziness, security checks, caching, logging or remote access without touching the real class or the callers.

Everyday analogies

  • Cheque or UPI: it stands in for cash and the bank decides whether to release money.
  • Company receptionist: you reach the manager only if the receptionist lets you in.
  • Power of attorney: someone acts on your behalf but within limits.

Kinds of proxy

  • Virtual proxy: creates the expensive object only when first needed (lazy loading).
  • Protection proxy: checks permissions before forwarding.
  • Remote proxy: represents an object in another process or machine (RMI stub, REST client).
  • Caching / smart-reference proxy: remembers results, counts references, logs calls.

Where you see it in Java / JDK / Spring

  • java.lang.reflect.Proxy creates proxies at runtime from interfaces (JDK dynamic proxy).
  • Collections.synchronizedMap style wrappers and RMI stubs (java.rmi).
  • Hibernate lazy loading: an entity reference is a generated subclass proxy that loads its row on first access.
  • Spring AOP: @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @Secured work because Spring injects a proxy (JDK proxy or CGLIB subclass) instead of your bean.

Structure

Client ---> Subject (interface)
                ^            ^
                |            |
          RealSubject  <---- Proxy  (has-a RealSubject, same interface)

When to use / when NOT to use

  • Use it for lazy loading, access control, caching, logging, or hiding network calls behind a normal interface.
  • Do NOT use it when a simple if inside the class is enough and there is only one such concern.
  • Do NOT forget the cost: hidden remote calls look like cheap local calls, which is dangerous in loops.

Sample: a lazy report proxy

Building a report is slow. The proxy creates it on the first show() call only, so a program that never shows the report never pays for it.

intermediate.content:
Sample 1: protection proxy

What it shows: the same interface with a role check in front of the real account. Why: security rules stay out of the business class and cannot be forgotten by a caller, because callers only receive the proxy.

Sample 2: JDK dynamic proxy for logging and timing

What it shows: one InvocationHandler that logs every call of any interface. Why: hand-written proxies need one class per interface; a dynamic proxy generates the class at runtime, which is how Spring AOP and many mocking libraries work.

Sample 3: rate-limiting proxy (smart reference)

What it shows: a proxy that counts calls and refuses after a quota. Why: API clients and gateways protect a scarce resource this way, and the real service stays unaware.

Sample 4: remote proxy with a hidden network call

What it shows: a local-looking interface whose proxy "serializes" the request to a fake server. Why: RMI stubs, gRPC stubs and Feign clients do exactly this; the caller writes weather.today(...) and never sees the transport.

Common mistakes

  • Self-invocation in Spring: a method calling another method of the same bean bypasses the proxy, so @Transactional or @Cacheable on the inner method does nothing.
  • Comparing with == or getClass(): a proxy is a different class from the target.
  • JDK dynamic proxies need an interface; for classes Spring uses CGLIB, which cannot proxy final classes or methods.
  • Making a lazy proxy that is not thread safe, creating the real object twice.
  • Hiding expensive remote calls behind innocent-looking getters and calling them in loops.

Proxy vs Decorator vs Adapter vs Facade

PatternInterfaceWho creates the wrapped objectTypical purpose
ProxySame as subjectOften the proxy (lazy, remote)Control access, lifecycle, location
DecoratorSame as componentThe client passes it inAdd behaviour, stackable
AdapterDifferentClient or adapterMake it compatible
FacadeNew simplifiedFacadeSimplify a subsystem

expert.content:
Real-time example 1: a generic caching proxy

One dynamic proxy factory that caches the result of any read-only method by method name and arguments. Business code stays free of cache logic; the hit counter shows the saving. This is the core of what Spring's @Cacheable does.

Real-time example 2: how Spring-style @Transactional works

A custom annotation plus a dynamic proxy that begins a "transaction" before methods marked @Tx, commits on success and rolls back when an exception escapes. This is a simplified version of what Spring's transaction proxy does around your service bean.

Sample mini project: secure document vault

Three proxies in one chain: a security proxy (who may read), an audit proxy (who did what) and a lazy loader for the heavy document body. The real Vault knows none of this.

Testing, Spring and performance notes

  • Testing: test the real subject without the proxy, then test the proxy with a stub subject (does it forward? does it block when it should? is the lazy object created once?). For dynamic proxies, assert on the recorded calls.
  • Spring: understand the two proxy types. JDK proxies need an interface; CGLIB (the default for classes in Spring Boot) subclasses your bean, so classes and methods must not be final. Calls made through this skip the proxy; fix by moving the method to another bean.
  • Hibernate: a lazy entity is a proxy; reading it after the session closes throws LazyInitializationException. Fetch what you need inside the transaction (join fetch, DTO projection).
  • Performance: reflection-based proxies cost a few hundred nanoseconds per call and block inlining; negligible next to I/O. Caching proxies need eviction and a bounded size or they leak memory.

Anti-patterns

  • Proxy hell: proxies of proxies where no one knows which layer applied which rule.
  • Logging full request bodies in a logging proxy, leaking secrets or personal data.
  • A cache proxy with no invalidation, serving stale prices indefinitely.

interviewQA: What is the Proxy pattern?

A structural pattern where a stand-in object with the same interface controls access to a real object. The proxy can delay creation, check permissions, cache, log or forward the call to a remote object.
Name the main types of proxy.
Virtual (lazy creation), protection (access control), remote (local representative of a remote object), and smart reference or caching (counting, logging, caching).
What is a JDK dynamic proxy and how does it differ from CGLIB?

java.lang.reflect.Proxy generates, at runtime, a class implementing given interfaces and routes all calls to an InvocationHandler. CGLIB generates a subclass of a concrete class instead, so it works without interfaces but cannot handle final classes or methods.
Why does @Transactional sometimes not work when a method calls another method of the same class?

Spring applies the behaviour in a proxy around the bean. A call through this goes straight to the target and bypasses the proxy, so the advice never runs. Move the method to another bean or inject the proxy.
Proxy vs Decorator?

Both wrap an object with the same interface. A decorator adds behaviour and is composed by the client; a proxy controls access to the object and often creates or locates it itself. The intent differs more than the structure.
How does Hibernate use the Proxy pattern?

getReference and lazy associations return a generated proxy subclass holding only the id; the SQL runs when you first call a getter other than getId. Outside an open session this causes LazyInitializationException.

topics.name: Bridge Pattern

beginner.content:
The Bridge Pattern decouples an abstraction from its implementation so the two can vary independently - instead of one growing inheritance tree, you split it into two smaller, separately-extensible hierarchies connected by composition.

Real-Life Example:

  • A TV remote (abstraction) working with different TV brands (implementation) - the remote's buttons stay the same regardless of which brand it controls
  • A universal charger (abstraction) working with different phone brands' charging circuits
  • A payment app (abstraction) working with different payment gateway implementations

Why do we need Bridge?

  • When a class varies along two independent dimensions (e.g. shape type AND color), plain inheritance forces a subclass per combination (RedCircle, GreenCircle, RedSquare, GreenSquare...) - this explodes quickly
  • Bridge splits the two dimensions into separate hierarchies joined by a reference, so either side can grow without touching the other

In one minute

A Bridge splits one big class into two separate hierarchies that can grow independently: the abstraction (what the client uses, e.g. a notification type) and the implementor (how the work is done, e.g. SMS or email). The abstraction holds a reference to an implementor and delegates to it. This avoids a class explosion: 3 notification types and 4 channels need 3 + 4 = 7 classes, not 3 x 4 = 12.

Everyday analogies

  • Remote control and TV: any remote (basic, smart) can work with any device (TV, AC, music system) through a shared button protocol.
  • Light switch and bulb: you can change the switch design or the bulb type independently.
  • Driver and car: a driver (abstraction) can use any vehicle (implementation) that has pedals and a wheel.

Where you see it in Java / JDK / Spring

  • JDBC: DriverManager / Connection (abstraction) and vendor drivers (implementors) are developed separately.
  • AWT: java.awt.Component classes delegate to platform peer objects.
  • SLF4J: the logging API and the binding to Logback or Log4j.
  • Spring's PlatformTransactionManager, and JpaVendorAdapter separate "what" from "which vendor".

Structure

Abstraction  ---has-a-->  Implementor (interface)
     ^                         ^           ^
RefinedAbstraction        ConcreteImplA  ConcreteImplB

   (what to do)   ====bridge====   (how it is done)

When to use / when NOT to use

  • Use it when a class varies along two independent dimensions (type x platform, shape x colour, report x format).
  • Use it to swap the implementation at runtime or to hide it from clients.
  • Do NOT use it when there is only one dimension; a plain interface and implementations is enough.
  • Do NOT use it up front "just in case"; introduce it when the second dimension actually appears.

Sample: notification types times channels

Two message types (alert, reminder) work over two channels (SMS, email). Adding a push channel later needs one new class and no change to the message types.

expert.content:
Bridge vs Adapter

Both use composition and both involve an interface, but the intent differs: Adapter is applied after the fact to make two already-existing, incompatible interfaces work together; Bridge is designed up front so an abstraction and its implementation can be developed and extended independently from day one.

Real-World Usage

JDBC is a textbook real Bridge: your Java code programs against the abstraction (java.sql.Connection, Statement), while each database vendor ships its own driver as the implementation side - swapping MySQL for PostgreSQL never requires changing your application code.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does Bridge solve?Class explosion when a type has two or more independently varying dimensions - it splits them into separate hierarchies joined by composition
Bridge vs Adapter - what's the real difference?Adapter retrofits incompatible interfaces after the fact; Bridge is designed up front to let abstraction and implementation evolve independently
Give a real JDK/framework example of BridgeJDBC - Connection/Statement is the abstraction, each vendor's driver is the implementation

Real-time example 1: cross-platform UI toolkit (the AWT idea)

Widgets (button, checkbox) are the abstraction; platform peers (desktop, web) are the implementors. Application code builds widgets once. To support a mobile theme you add one peer class and touch no widget.

Real-time example 2: alerting with severity levels and fallback channels

The severity (info, critical) decides which channels get the message; each channel decides how to send it. A critical alert tries every channel in order until one succeeds, which is a real operations pattern (pager, then call, then SMS).

Sample mini project: report generator, report type x output format

Two report types and three formats give six outputs from only five classes (and a new format costs one class). Each report only describes its rows; the format decides how they look.

Testing, Spring and performance notes

  • Testing: test each implementor against the implementor contract (a shared abstract test class), and test each abstraction with a fake implementor that records calls. You test n + m things instead of n x m combinations.
  • Spring: inject the implementor into the abstraction through the constructor, choose it with @Profile, @ConditionalOnProperty or a @Qualifier. Typical pairs are NotificationService with MessageSender beans, or a ReportService with ExportFormat beans collected as a Map<String, ExportFormat>.
  • Performance: one extra indirection per call, negligible. Keep implementors stateless where possible so one instance is shared.
  • Combine with Abstract Factory when the implementor must be created consistently for a whole family of abstractions.

Anti-patterns

  • Leaky bridge: the abstraction casts the implementor to a concrete class to use a special feature.
  • Bridge to nowhere: an implementor interface with exactly one implementation that will never change.
  • Duplicating the same logic in every implementor instead of lifting it into the abstraction (template-method style).

intermediate.content:
Sample 1: shapes bridged to renderers

What it shows: the classic two hierarchies, shapes (circle, rectangle) and renderers (text, SVG-like markup). Why: a new renderer (say, JSON) works with every shape automatically, and a new shape works with every renderer.

Sample 2: remote control with a refined abstraction

What it shows: a basic remote and an advanced remote (extends the abstraction) driving a TV or a radio (implementors). Why: refinements of the abstraction add features (mute) using only the implementor interface, so they work for every device.

Sample 3: a JDBC-style driver bridge with runtime switching

What it shows: a Repository abstraction that can switch its storage driver while running. Why: this is the idea behind JDBC: your code is written once against the abstraction and the vendor driver is chosen by configuration.

Common mistakes

  • Premature bridge: splitting into two hierarchies when only one dimension exists.
  • Choosing the wrong split: the implementor interface should contain primitive operations, the abstraction the higher-level operations built from them.
  • Letting the abstraction know the concrete implementor (casts, instanceof), which destroys the independence.
  • Making the implementor interface too wide, so every new implementor must write dozens of methods.
  • Confusing it with Adapter: Bridge is planned up front for independent variation; Adapter is a fix after the fact.

Bridge vs Adapter vs Strategy vs Abstract Factory

PatternWhen designedCore ideaTypical sign
BridgeUp frontTwo hierarchies vary independentlyAbstraction subclasses plus implementor subclasses
AdapterAfter the factMake existing classes fitOne wrapper per incompatible class
StrategyAny timeSwap one algorithmContext plus interchangeable strategy; no abstraction hierarchy
Abstract FactoryUp frontCreate families of related objectsOften used together with Bridge to create the implementor

interviewQA: What is the Bridge pattern?
It decouples an abstraction from its implementation so the two can vary independently. The abstraction holds a reference to an implementor interface and delegates the low-level work to it.
What problem does Bridge solve?
The class explosion caused by inheritance on two independent dimensions. With m abstractions and n implementations, inheritance gives m x n classes, Bridge gives m + n.
How is Bridge different from Adapter?
Bridge is designed up front so abstraction and implementation evolve separately. Adapter is applied afterwards to make an existing incompatible class fit an expected interface.
How is Bridge different from Strategy?
Structurally similar (composition with an interface), but Strategy swaps one algorithm inside a context. Bridge separates a whole hierarchy of abstractions from a hierarchy of implementations.
Give a real Java example of Bridge.
JDBC: your code uses Connection and Statement (abstraction) and the database vendor driver is the implementor. AWT component and peer, and SLF4J API with its bindings, follow the same idea.
How would you add a new output format or platform without changing existing code?
Add one new class implementing the implementor interface and register or inject it. All existing abstractions work with it unchanged, which respects the Open/Closed principle.

topics.name: Composite Pattern

beginner.content:
The Composite Pattern lets you treat individual objects and groups of objects through the same interface, so client code doesn't need to know whether it's dealing with a single item or a whole tree of them.

Real-Life Example:

  • A file system - a File and a Folder (which can contain Files and other Folders) both expose the same "get size" operation
  • An org chart - an individual employee and an entire department both respond to "list all members"
  • A UI toolkit - a single Button and a Panel full of widgets both respond to "render"

Why do we need Composite?

  • Represent part-whole (tree) hierarchies naturally
  • Let client code call the same method on a leaf or an entire branch without an if/else check for "is this one item or many?"

In one minute

A Composite lets you treat a single object (a leaf) and a group of objects (a composite node) through the same interface. A composite holds children that may themselves be composites, so you can build a tree and run one operation (size(), price(), render()) over the whole tree with a single call. The client does not need if (isGroup) checks.

Everyday analogies

  • Folders and files: a folder holds files and other folders; "size" works on both.
  • Army: an order given to a general passes down through divisions to every soldier.
  • Gift box: a box may contain items and smaller boxes; the total price is the sum of everything inside.

Where you see it in Java / JDK / Spring

  • java.awt.Container contains Components, and a Container is itself a Component. Swing's JPanel and JavaFX's Parent/Node work the same way.
  • DOM trees (org.w3c.dom.Node), javax.swing.tree.TreeNode.
  • Spring Security's CompositeFilter, Spring's CompositePropertySource and Jackson's JsonNode tree.
  • java.util.Map.putAll is not a composite, but a collection of collections often is.

Structure

Component (interface: operation())
   ^                    ^
   |                    |
 Leaf              Composite --has many--> Component
 operation()       operation() { for child: child.operation() }

Tree:   Box
        +-- Book
        +-- Box
            +-- Pen
            +-- Notebook

When to use / when NOT to use

  • Use it when the data is naturally a part-whole tree and clients should ignore the difference between one and many.
  • Do NOT use it when the structure is flat; a plain list is simpler.
  • Be careful when leaves and groups really need very different operations; a shared interface may become awkward.

Sample: a gift box that totals its price

Items and boxes both implement Priced. The outer box does not care what is inside; it asks every child for its price.

expert.content:
When to Use Composite

Reach for Composite whenever your domain is naturally a tree and you find yourself writing "if this is a single item, do X; if it's a group, loop and do X to each" - Composite eliminates that branch entirely by giving both cases the same interface.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What structural problem does Composite solve?Letting client code treat a single object and a group/tree of objects uniformly through one shared interface
Give an example of Composite in the JDKjava.awt.Container extends Component - a Container can hold other Components, including other Containers
What's the trade-off of Composite?Leaf-only operations (like "add child") must still exist on the shared interface even though a leaf can't meaningfully support them, unless you accept throwing UnsupportedOperationException

Real-time example 1: UI component tree with propagating state

A form is a panel of panels and widgets. render() draws recursively as HTML-like text, and setEnabled(false) on any panel disables everything beneath it. This mirrors how Swing, JavaFX and web DOMs behave.

Real-time example 2: composable business rules (specification tree)

Discount eligibility rules are leaves; AND, OR and NOT are composites that combine other rules. Operations teams can build new rules from small ones without touching code that evaluates them. The same shape appears in Spring Data's Specification and in query builders.

Sample mini project: holiday itinerary pricing

A trip is a tree: days contain activities and optional sub-groups. Every node reports its cost, and a group may apply a discount to everything beneath it. The program prints an indented price breakdown.

Testing, Spring and performance notes

  • Testing: build small trees by hand (empty composite, single leaf, nested three levels, a very wide one) and assert totals. Test that adding a child sets the parent and that cycles are rejected.
  • Spring: a CompositeXxx bean that implements an interface and delegates to List<Xxx> (Spring injects all beans of a type) is the idiomatic composite: for example a CompositeHealthIndicator or your own CompositeNotifier that sends through every registered Notifier. Use @Primary on the composite so callers get it by default.
  • Performance: recursion cost is O(n) per full traversal. Cache aggregates (size, price) when the tree is read far more than it is written, and invalidate on child changes up the parent chain. For very large trees use iterative traversal or streams with care (deep recursion in flatMap is fine, but mutation while streaming is not).
  • Concurrency: make trees immutable (build once, share) or guard structural changes with a lock.

Anti-patterns

  • Type-checking composite: clients keep writing if (node instanceof Folder), which defeats the pattern; add the needed operation to the interface instead.
  • Fat component interface full of methods that make sense for only one kind of node.
  • Using Composite for a flat list "because it might become a tree".

intermediate.content:
Sample 1: file system with size, count and search

What it shows: three operations (size, file count, find by extension) implemented recursively over the same tree. Why: each node answers for itself, so adding a new operation only needs a loop in the composite and a one-liner in the leaf.

Sample 2: restaurant menu tree with depth-aware printing

What it shows: a menu made of menus and dishes, printed with indentation and filtered to vegetarian items. Why: the same traversal supports display, filtering and counting; this is the classic "menu of menus" use case.

Sample 3: org chart with parent links and flattening with streams

What it shows: a composite where each node knows its parent, so it can print its path to the root, and a stream() method that flattens the whole tree. Why: navigation upward and "give me all nodes as a list" are the two things real tree APIs always need.

Common mistakes

  • Transparent vs safe: putting add/remove on the shared interface lets you call them on a leaf (they must throw or do nothing). Safe designs keep them only on the composite, at the price of a cast or a separate type.
  • Cycles: adding a node to its own descendant makes recursion loop forever. Check ancestors before attaching.
  • Recomputing expensive totals on every call in a deep tree; cache and invalidate if profiling shows a cost.
  • Exposing the internal children list so clients can modify the tree without the parent link being updated.
  • Deep recursion on very deep trees leading to StackOverflowError; use an explicit stack or iterative traversal.

Composite vs Decorator vs Iterator vs Visitor

PatternRelationship to CompositeDifference
Composite-One node holds many children (tree), same interface
DecoratorSimilar structureWraps exactly one component to add behaviour; no "many children" aggregation
IteratorOften used with itWalks the tree without exposing the structure
VisitorOften used with itAdds new operations to the tree without changing node classes
Chain of ResponsibilityCan use parent linksPasses a request up the tree until a node handles it

interviewQA: What is the Composite pattern?
A structural pattern that composes objects into tree structures and lets clients treat individual objects (leaves) and compositions of objects uniformly through a common interface.
What are the participants of Composite?
Component (common interface), Leaf (no children, does the real work), Composite (stores children and forwards operations to them) and the Client which uses only the Component interface.
Transparent vs safe composite: what is the trade-off?

Transparent puts add/remove in the Component interface, so clients treat everything uniformly but leaves must reject child operations at runtime. Safe puts child management only in the Composite, which is type safe but clients sometimes need to know which kind of node they hold.
Give Composite examples in Java.
AWT Container and Component, Swing JPanel, JavaFX Node and Parent, the DOM Node tree, Jackson JsonNode, and Spring composite beans such as CompositeFilter or CompositePropertySource.
How do you avoid infinite recursion in a composite?
Reject attaching a node to itself or to one of its descendants (walk the parent chain before adding), keep trees acyclic by design, and for deep trees use iterative traversal instead of recursion.
How do Composite and Visitor work together?
Composite gives the tree structure; Visitor adds new operations (export, validate, price) as separate classes that traverse it, so you do not have to change every node class for each new operation.

topics.name: Flyweight Pattern

beginner.content:
The Flyweight Pattern reduces memory usage by sharing common state across many similar objects instead of storing that state redundantly in each one.

Real-Life Example:

  • A text editor - every occurrence of the letter "A" in a document can share ONE glyph/font object instead of each character owning its own copy
  • A game with thousands of trees on a map - the 3D model/texture (shared) is reused; only each tree's x/y position (unique) is stored per instance

Intrinsic vs Extrinsic State

  • Intrinsic state - shared, immutable, stored once inside the flyweight object (e.g. the character's font/shape)
  • Extrinsic state - unique per usage, passed in from outside at the point of use, NOT stored in the flyweight (e.g. the character's x/y position on screen)

In one minute

A Flyweight saves memory by sharing one object among thousands of uses instead of creating a new one each time. The object's data is split in two: intrinsic state (shared, immutable, stored inside the flyweight, e.g. the icon image) and extrinsic state (different per use, passed in by the caller, e.g. x and y position). A flyweight factory hands out the shared instances from a cache.

Everyday analogies

  • Library copies: one book title shared by many readers over time, not one new book per reader.
  • Rubber stamps: one stamp, used on thousands of pages; the page (extrinsic) changes, the stamp (intrinsic) does not.
  • Font glyphs: the letter shape "a" exists once; the document only stores where each "a" goes.

Where you see it in Java / JDK / Spring

  • Integer.valueOf(int) caches -128 to 127; Boolean.valueOf, Byte.valueOf and Character.valueOf do too.
  • String literals and String.intern() use the string constant pool.
  • Enums: each constant is a single shared instance.
  • java.util.Collections.emptyList(), List.of() with no args and Optional.empty() return shared singletons.
  • Connection and thread pools share expensive objects (related idea: object pool, but pooled objects are checked out, flyweights are shared at the same time).

Structure

Client ---> FlyweightFactory ---has---> cache: Map<key, Flyweight>
   |                                          |
   +-- passes extrinsic state -------> Flyweight.operation(extrinsic)

1,000,000 map markers  -->  3 Icon objects + 1,000,000 (x, y) pairs

When to use / when NOT to use

  • Use it when you need a huge number of similar objects and memory is the bottleneck (profile first).
  • Use it when most of the object's state can be made immutable and shared.
  • Do NOT use it when there are few objects, or when objects are mostly unique; you add complexity and gain nothing.
  • Do NOT share mutable objects: a change by one user would corrupt all the others.

Sample: map markers sharing icons

Three icon types are created once. A thousand markers only store a reference and a position, and the output proves that the icons are the same objects.

expert.content:
A Built-In JDK Flyweight: Integer Caching

Integer.valueOf(int) caches and reuses Integer objects for values -128 to 127 - this is exactly the Flyweight idea baked into the JDK itself, which is why Integer a = 100; Integer b = 100; a == b is true, but the same comparison for 1000 is false (outside the cached range, a new object is created each time).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does Flyweight solve?Excessive memory usage when creating a very large number of similar objects, by sharing their common (intrinsic) state instead of duplicating it
Difference between intrinsic and extrinsic state?Intrinsic state is shared and stored inside the flyweight; extrinsic state is unique per use and supplied by the caller at call time, never stored in the flyweight
Name a Flyweight example already in the JDKInteger.valueOf() caching Integer objects in the range -128 to 127

Real-time example 1: game tile map

A 1,000 by 1,000 map has a million cells, but only four tile types. The map stores one small reference per cell, and each shared TileType carries the heavy data (name, movement cost). This is how real engines store terrain.

Real-time example 2: invoice lines sharing product and tax data

An invoice batch has 30,000 lines. Product description and GST slab repeat constantly, so lines keep only references plus quantity (extrinsic). The program verifies identity and computes totals with the shared data.

Sample mini project: chess set with shared pieces

There are 32 pieces on a board but only 12 kinds (6 types x 2 colours). Each kind is a flyweight; the board stores references by square. The program lays out the starting position and reports how many objects were really created.

Testing, Spring and performance notes

  • Testing: assert identity (assertSame) for two requests with the same key, assert that flyweights are immutable (final fields, no setters) and that the factory is thread safe with a concurrent test as in the sample above.
  • Spring: singleton-scoped beans are flyweights of a kind: one shared stateless instance serves every request, which is why beans must not hold per-request state (that is the extrinsic part, pass it as method arguments). Spring's ConcurrentReferenceHashMap and Caffeine caches are common choices for a flyweight pool with eviction.
  • Performance: measure with a profiler or JOL before and after. Gains are largest when intrinsic data is heavy and duplicates are many; the cost is a hash lookup per creation and the risk of memory held by the pool. Keep keys small and well-hashed (records are ideal).
  • Java tools that help: records for immutable flyweights, computeIfAbsent for atomic creation, and primitive arrays (instead of objects) when even references are too heavy.

Anti-patterns

  • Hidden global cache: a static map nobody can clear, causing leaks in long running servers and flaky tests.
  • Flyweight with identity semantics: code that relies on == for equality of values that are not guaranteed to be pooled.
  • Premature optimisation: introducing sharing before measuring a real memory problem.

intermediate.content:
Sample 1: characters in a text editor

What it shows: a document of 40 characters that only needs a handful of shared Glyph objects, because the glyph (character plus font) is intrinsic while the position in the text is extrinsic. Why: this is the original example from the Gang of Four book and scales to megabyte documents.

Sample 2: flyweights already inside the JDK

What it shows: the Integer cache boundary, string pooling and Boolean.valueOf. Why: interviewers love this; it explains why == on two Integer objects works for 127 and breaks for 128, and why you must use equals.

Sample 3: counting the memory saving

What it shows: the same 100,000 forest trees built twice, once with a new species object per tree and once with a shared one, and a rough byte estimate. Why: it turns "saves memory" into a number you can reason about. (The figures are estimates for the data fields, not an exact JVM measurement.)

Sample 4: a thread-safe flyweight factory

What it shows: eight threads requesting the same three shared objects from a ConcurrentHashMap. Why: a plain HashMap factory can create duplicates or corrupt itself under concurrency; computeIfAbsent makes creation atomic, so exactly one instance per key exists.

Common mistakes

  • Mutable flyweight: any setter on shared state is a bug waiting to happen. Make flyweights final with final fields.
  • Storing extrinsic state inside the flyweight (for example the position), which defeats the sharing.
  • Applying it without measuring: a few hundred objects do not need it, and it makes code harder to read.
  • An unbounded factory cache that grows forever (memory leak); use a bounded key space, a WeakHashMap, or a cache with eviction.
  • Comparing boxed values with == and relying on the cache range; always use equals.

Flyweight vs Singleton vs Object Pool vs Prototype

PatternHow many instancesShared at the same time?Mutable?
FlyweightOne per distinct intrinsic stateYes, by many clientsNo, immutable
SingletonExactly oneYesUsually yes
Object PoolA fixed set of reusable objectsNo, one borrower at a timeYes, reset on return
PrototypeMany copies of a templateNo, each is a cloneYes

interviewQA: What is the Flyweight pattern?

A structural pattern that reduces memory use by sharing objects. Common immutable data (intrinsic state) lives in a shared flyweight; varying data (extrinsic state) is supplied by the client at each call.
Explain intrinsic vs extrinsic state with an example.

In a text editor a Glyph holds the character and font (intrinsic, shared). The position of each character in the document is extrinsic and passed to draw(). Intrinsic state is context-independent, extrinsic state is context-dependent.
Why does Integer 127 == 127 work but 128 == 128 not?
Integer.valueOf caches instances for -128 to 127 (a flyweight). Outside the range each autoboxing creates a new object, so == compares references. Always compare boxed values with equals.
Why must flyweights be immutable?
They are shared by many clients simultaneously. If one client changed the shared state, every other user would see the change. Immutability also makes them thread safe without locks.
How is Flyweight different from Singleton and Object Pool?

Singleton has one instance of a class, usually mutable. Flyweight has one instance per distinct intrinsic state, immutable and shared concurrently. An object pool lends out reusable mutable objects one borrower at a time.
How do you make a flyweight factory thread safe?
Use ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent (atomic per key) or an initialisation-on-demand holder for a fixed set, and keep the flyweights immutable.

topics.name: Observer Pattern

beginner.content:
Observer Pattern defines a one-to-many dependency between objects, so that when one object (the "subject") changes state, all its dependents ("observers") are notified and updated automatically.

Real-Life Example:

  • YouTube channel subscribers get notified whenever the channel uploads a new video
  • Newspaper/magazine subscription - all subscribers get the new edition automatically
  • Java's own java.util.Observer (legacy) and any GUI event-listener system

Why do we need Observer?

  • To notify multiple dependent objects about a state change without tightly coupling them to the subject
  • To let observers be added/removed at runtime without changing the subject's code
  • It's the foundation of event-driven and reactive programming (pub-sub systems)

In one minute

The Observer pattern lets one object, the subject (also called publisher), keep a list of observers (subscribers) and tell all of them whenever its state changes. The subject only knows that each observer has an update method, so you can add or remove observers without touching the subject.

More real-life analogies

  • Railway platform announcements: one announcer, many waiting passengers who react in their own way.
  • Weather alert SMS: the met office changes a forecast and every registered phone gets a message.
  • Stock-market ticker: a price change is pushed to every trader screen and every alert rule.

Where you see it in Java and Spring

  • java.beans.PropertyChangeListener and PropertyChangeSupport for bound properties.
  • Swing and JavaFX listeners such as ActionListener and ChangeListener.
  • java.util.Observable and Observer (deprecated since Java 9, prefer the alternatives).
  • java.util.concurrent.Flow and SubmissionPublisher for reactive streams.
  • Spring ApplicationEvent, ApplicationListener and @EventListener.

Structure

Subject (Publisher)             Observer (Subscriber)
+------------------+  1..*     +------------------+
| attach(o)        |---------->| update(data)     |
| detach(o)        |           +------------------+
| notifyObservers()|                    ^
+------------------+          +---------+---------+
        ^                     |                   |
 ConcreteSubject         SmsObserver        DisplayObserver

When to use / when NOT to use

  • Use it when a change in one object must update an unknown or changing number of other objects.
  • Use it for event systems, UI updates, notifications and audit hooks.
  • Avoid it when there is exactly one fixed receiver; a plain method call is simpler.
  • Avoid it when the order of notifications really matters; observers should not depend on each other.

Small program: weather office with lambdas

Because the observer interface has one method, a lambda or Consumer can act as an observer. No extra classes are needed.

intermediate.content:
Push versus pull notification

WHAT: two ways to hand data to observers. In push the subject sends the new values as arguments. In pull the subject sends only itself and the observer asks for what it needs.

WHY: push is simple but forces every observer to receive data it may not need. Pull keeps the interface stable when the subject grows new fields.

Generic observer with unsubscribe handle

WHAT: a reusable ObsTopic<T> where subscribe returns a Runnable that removes the listener.

WHY: forgetting to unsubscribe is the number one memory leak in observer code: the subject holds a strong reference to every listener. Returning a handle makes cleanup easy and explicit.

JDK PropertyChangeSupport

WHAT: the JDK already ships an observer toolkit for bean properties. PropertyChangeSupport manages listeners and fires an event only when the old and new values differ.

WHY: in real projects you often reuse this instead of hand-writing the list handling.

Topic-based event bus

WHAT: observers subscribe to a named topic instead of to a single subject, so one bus serves many kinds of news.

WHY: publishers and subscribers no longer know each other at all; this is the idea behind message brokers and Spring events.

Common mistakes

  • Memory leak: observers never removed keep the subject (and everything they reference) alive. Always provide unsubscribe, or hold WeakReference observers.
  • ConcurrentModificationException: an observer that unsubscribes while the list is being iterated. Iterate over a copy or use CopyOnWriteArrayList.
  • Update storms and cycles: observer A changes the subject, which notifies A again. Guard with a flag or compare old and new values.
  • One failing observer stops the rest: wrap each call in try/catch so one exception does not block the others.
  • Depending on notification order: the order is an implementation detail, do not rely on it.

Observer compared with similar patterns

PatternRelationshipKey difference
Observerone subject to many observerssubject knows its observers directly
Mediatormany colleagues through one hubhub coordinates and contains logic
Pub-Sub / Event Buspublishers and subscribers via a brokerfull decoupling through a channel
Chain of Responsibilityone request passed along handlersusually one handler acts, not all

expert.content:
Real-time example 1: order events with error isolation

An e-commerce order service publishes typed events. Inventory, billing and email listeners react. A faulty listener must never break checkout, so each call is isolated and failures are reported.

Real-time example 2: re-entrant safe notifications

A seat-booking subject has an observer that reacts to a change by changing the subject again (it releases a waiting-list seat). Notifying immediately would recurse. This version queues events and drains them in order, which keeps the output predictable.

Sample mini project: Fort ticket dashboard

Several small classes work together: a subject (ObsTicketOffice), three observers (a live display, a revenue tracker and a sold-out alert) and a demo that prints a readable result.

Thread safety, testing and Spring notes

  • Thread safety: use CopyOnWriteArrayList for read-mostly listener lists; never call unknown observer code while holding a lock (risk of deadlock). Publish from a snapshot of the state.
  • Asynchronous delivery: hand events to an ExecutorService if observers are slow, but then ordering and error handling become your job.
  • Testing: register a recording lambda (it adds to a list) and assert on the list; test unsubscribe and exception isolation explicitly.
  • Spring: inject ApplicationEventPublisher and call publishEvent(new OrderPlacedEvent(...)); listeners use @EventListener. Add @TransactionalEventListener to react only after a commit and @Async for background handling.

Anti-patterns

  • Event spaghetti: dozens of events triggering each other so nobody can follow the flow.
  • Fat events that carry the whole domain graph, coupling observers to subject internals.
  • Business-critical logic hidden in a listener that can be silently unregistered.

interviewQA: What problem does Observer solve?

It removes tight coupling between an object whose state changes and the objects that must react. The subject only knows an observer interface, so observers can be added or removed at runtime without changing it.
Push or pull model: how do you choose?

Push sends the data with the notification, which is simple but may send unneeded data. Pull passes the subject so the observer fetches only what it needs, which keeps the interface stable when the subject evolves.
How can Observer cause a memory leak, and how do you avoid it?

The subject holds strong references to its observers, so an observer that is never unsubscribed cannot be garbage collected (the lapsed listener problem). Provide unsubscribe, return a removal handle, or store WeakReferences.
How do you make notification safe when observers unsubscribe during the callback?
Iterate over a copy of the list or use CopyOnWriteArrayList so the iteration is not affected by concurrent modification.
Why was java.util.Observable deprecated?
It is a class, so a subject cannot extend anything else, setChanged is protected, it is not thread safe and gives no event typing. Use PropertyChangeSupport, Flow, or your own listener interfaces.
What is the difference between Observer and Pub-Sub?
In Observer the subject knows its observers directly. In Pub-Sub a broker or channel sits between publishers and subscribers, so they never know each other and can even run in different processes.
How does Spring implement Observer?

ApplicationEventPublisher publishes events, and beans annotated with @EventListener (or implementing ApplicationListener) receive them. Events can be handled asynchronously with @Async or after commit with @TransactionalEventListener.

topics.name: Chain of Responsibility Pattern

beginner.content:
Chain of Responsibility lets you pass a request along a chain of handlers. Each handler decides either to process the request or pass it to the next handler.

Real-Life Example:

  • ATM cash dispenser — handles request using 2000, 500, 100 notes in a chain
  • Tech support escalation — L1 support tries first, then L2, then L3
  • Leave approval — Manager approves small leaves, Director approves longer ones

Why do we need it?

  • Decouples sender of a request from its receivers
  • Multiple objects get a chance to handle the request
  • New handlers can be added without changing existing code

Basic Structure:

  • Step 1: Create abstract Handler with a setNext() method
  • Step 2: Create concrete handlers that either handle or forward the request
  • Step 3: Client builds the chain and sends request to the first handler

In one minute

In Chain of Responsibility a request travels along a line of handlers. Each handler either deals with the request or passes it to its successor. The sender does not know which handler will finally process it, and handlers can be re-ordered or added without changing the sender.

More real-life analogies

  • Bank loan approval: clerk, manager, regional head. Small loans stop at the clerk, big ones climb the ladder.
  • Customer support levels: L1 agent, L2 engineer, L3 developer. The ticket moves up until someone can solve it.
  • Airport security: ticket check, baggage scan, body scan. Each stage can stop the passenger or let them continue.

Where you see it in Java and Spring

  • Servlet javax.servlet.Filter and FilterChain.doFilter(request, response).
  • Spring Security SecurityFilterChain and Spring MVC HandlerInterceptor.
  • java.util.logging.Logger passing records to parent loggers; Log4j and Logback appender chains.
  • The try / catch blocks of Java: an exception goes up the call stack until some handler catches it.
  • java.util.function.Function.andThen style pipelines are a functional cousin.

Structure

Client --> [Handler A] --next--> [Handler B] --next--> [Handler C]
              |                     |                     |
        handles or passes     handles or passes     handles or ends

abstract Handler { Handler next; handle(request) }

When to use / when NOT to use

  • Use it when more than one object may handle a request and the handler is not known in advance.
  • Use it for validation pipelines, approval workflows, request filters and event bubbling.
  • Use it when the set of handlers and their order should be configurable at runtime.
  • Avoid it when exactly one object always handles the request; a direct call is clearer.
  • Avoid very long chains where a request may fall off the end unhandled and nobody notices.

Small program: support ticket levels

Each level handles tickets up to its own severity and passes harder ones on. The last line reports what happens when nobody can handle the request.

expert.content:
ATM Cash Dispenser — Full Chain Example

A very common interview example: dispensing cash using the fewest number of currency notes, where each handler is responsible for one denomination and passes the remainder down the chain.

Servlet Filters — A Real Chain of Responsibility Example

The Java Servlet API's Filter mechanism is a textbook production use of Chain of Responsibility. Each filter processes the request/response and then decides whether to pass control to the next filter using FilterChain.doFilter().

Chain of Responsibility vs Decorator

Aspect Chain of Responsibility Decorator
Intent Pass request until someone handles it Add extra behavior/wrapping around an object
Execution Usually only ONE handler processes it (or a subset), can stop early Every decorator in the stack always executes
Structure Linked list of handlers Nested wrapper objects
Example Servlet Filters, Leave Approval, ATM Dispenser BufferedReader wrapping Reader, java.io streams

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting to call next handler — request silently gets dropped
  • Creating a circular chain (A → B → A), leading to infinite loops
  • Not having a default/terminal handler that guarantees the request is eventually handled

Interview Questions

#QuestionShort Answer
1What is Chain of Responsibility?A behavioral pattern that passes a request along a chain of handlers until one of them handles it
2What problem does it solve?Decouples the sender of a request from the specific object that will handle it
3Give a real Java framework example.Servlet Filters — each Filter decides whether to handle/modify the request and call chain.doFilter() to continue
4What's a common bug with this pattern?Forgetting to forward to the next handler, silently dropping the request
5Chain of Responsibility vs Decorator?CoR usually stops at the first handler that processes the request; Decorator always runs every wrapper in the stack
6How do you prevent infinite loops in a chain?Build the chain as a strict acyclic structure and always terminate with a handler that has next = null

Real-time example 1: HTTP-like request pipeline

A request goes through rate limiting, authentication and role authorization. Each stage returns a result, so the first failing stage produces a clear status code. This is how API gateways and Spring Security behave.

Real-time example 2: event bubbling in a UI tree

A click is offered first to the innermost widget; if it is not consumed it bubbles to its parent, as in Swing, JavaFX and the browser DOM. The chain here is the parent link of each widget.

Sample mini project: loan approval desk

A bank desk processes loan applications. The chain has a credit check, an amount-based approver ladder and a final audit trail. Several small classes cooperate and the demo prints a decision for each applicant.

Thread safety, testing and Spring notes

  • Thread safety: build the chain once and treat it as immutable; handlers must keep no per-request state in fields. Per-request data belongs in the request object or method arguments.
  • Testing: unit-test each handler alone with a fake next handler, then test the assembled chain for order and for the "nobody handles it" case.
  • Spring: Spring injects a List<Handler> of all beans of a type, sorted by @Order. Loop over that list instead of hand-linking. Spring Security uses an ordered SecurityFilterChain and MVC uses HandlerInterceptor.
  • Resilience: keep failure handling explicit, for example a final handler that logs unhandled requests.

Anti-patterns

  • God handler: one link with a huge if-else, which defeats the pattern.
  • Handlers that mutate shared global state and depend on running in a specific order.
  • Chains used where a Map lookup would do: if the handler can be chosen by a key, use a Map of strategies.

intermediate.content:
Approval workflow with a functional chain

WHAT: a leave or expense approval where each approver is a lambda-backed handler with its own limit.

WHY: shows that handlers do not need one class each. A small record plus a limit is enough, and the chain is built from a list.

Validation chain that collects every error

WHAT: a chain where each validator checks one rule and always passes control on, so all problems are collected.

WHY: a chain does not have to stop at the first handler. In validation you often want a full list of errors, not only the first one.

Logging levels chain

WHAT: a console logger, a file logger and an alert logger, each reacting to a minimum level. A message may be handled by several links.

WHY: this is the classic "pass it on even if I handled it" variant, used by log frameworks.

Servlet-style filter chain

WHAT: a mini FilterChain where each filter does work before and after the next one, like authentication, logging and compression filters.

WHY: this is the form you will meet in real web frameworks. A filter decides whether to call chain.next(), so it can also short-circuit the request.

Common mistakes

  • Infinite chain: linking a handler back to an earlier one creates a cycle. Build chains in one place and never reuse a node twice.
  • Request falls off the end: if no handler matches, nothing happens silently. Add a default last handler or throw an exception.
  • Forgetting to call next: a handler that handles the request but should also let others act must still forward it.
  • Order dependence hidden in code: authentication must run before authorization. Document the order and test it.
  • Stack depth: recursive chains with hundreds of links can overflow the stack; use a loop over a list.

Chain of Responsibility compared with similar patterns

PatternIdeaKey difference
Chain of Responsibilitypass a request along candidatessender does not know the receiver
Decoratorwrap an object to add behaviorevery wrapper acts, and the object keeps its interface
Commandturn a request into an objectone known receiver executes it
Observernotify all subscribersall observers react, not one of many
Strategychoose one algorithmthe client picks it, no passing along

interviewQA: What is Chain of Responsibility and what does it decouple?

A request is passed along a chain of handlers, and each one decides to handle it or forward it. It decouples the sender from the concrete receiver, because the sender only holds a reference to the first handler.
Does exactly one handler process a request?
Not necessarily. In the classic form the first capable handler stops the chain. In the pipeline form (servlet filters, loggers) many handlers act and each one forwards the request.
Where is it used in Java and Spring?
Servlet Filter and FilterChain, Spring Security SecurityFilterChain, Spring MVC HandlerInterceptor, java.util.logging parent loggers, and the exception propagation through catch blocks.
What happens if no handler can process the request?
It is silently dropped unless you handle it. Good designs add a default final handler or throw an exception so the failure is visible.
How do you avoid cycles and deep recursion in a chain?

Build the chain from an ordered list in one place and iterate with a loop or an index, instead of hand-linking nodes that can be linked twice. A list based chain also avoids stack overflow for very long chains.
How does it differ from Decorator?

A decorator always delegates to the wrapped object and adds behavior while keeping the same interface. A chain handler may stop the request and does not necessarily wrap anything; the purpose is selecting who handles it.
How would you test a chain?
Test each handler in isolation with a stub next handler, then test the full chain in order with representative requests, including the unhandled case and short-circuiting.

topics.name: Interpreter Pattern

beginner.content:
What is the Interpreter Pattern?

The Interpreter Pattern defines a way to evaluate language grammar or expressions. It represents each rule of the grammar as a class, and combines these classes to interpret sentences (expressions) in that language.

Real-Life Example:

  • A calculator that reads "3 + 5 * 2" and evaluates the result.
  • A traffic signal controller interpreting simple rule sentences like "IF car THEN stop".
  • A basic search engine interpreting boolean queries like "java AND spring".

Why do we need Interpreter Pattern?

  • To evaluate expressions written in a simple custom language or grammar.
  • To break a complex expression into smaller, manageable expression objects.
  • To make grammar rules easy to extend by adding new expression classes.

Basic Structure:

  • Expression (interface) — declares an interpret() method.
  • Terminal Expression — represents the basic elements of grammar (e.g., a number).
  • Non-Terminal Expression — represents rules combining other expressions (e.g., addition, multiplication).
  • Client — builds the expression tree and calls interpret().

How It Works — Step by Step

  • Every number (3, 5, 2) becomes a NumberExpression (Terminal Expression).
  • The multiplication "5 * 2" becomes a MultiplyExpression wrapping the two numbers.
  • The addition "3 + (5*2)" becomes an AddExpression wrapping the number and the multiply expression.
  • Calling interpret() on the outermost expression recursively evaluates the whole tree.

Expression Tree Diagram:

              AddExpression
              /           \\
      NumberExpression(3)   MultiplyExpression
                              /           \\
                    NumberExpression(5)  NumberExpression(2)

Each node "interprets itself" and passes the result up to its parent — this is a classic recursive tree evaluation.

In one minute

The Interpreter pattern gives you a way to evaluate sentences of a small language. You write one class per grammar rule. Terminal rules (a number, a variable) answer directly, and non-terminal rules (add, and, or) combine child expressions. Together the objects form an abstract syntax tree and calling interpret() on the root evaluates the whole sentence.

More real-life analogies

  • Sheet music: a musician reads symbols (the grammar) and turns them into sound.
  • Calculator: you type 2 + 3 * 4 and it knows the rules of arithmetic.
  • Road signs and Morse code: a fixed small vocabulary with fixed rules of meaning.

Where you see it in Java and Spring

  • java.util.regex.Pattern compiles a regular expression into a matcher tree.
  • java.text.Format and MessageFormat interpret format strings.
  • Spring Expression Language: SpelExpressionParser, Expression.getValue(context).
  • javax.el.ExpressionFactory (JSP / Jakarta Expression Language) and JPA query strings.
  • Ant / Gradle build scripts and SQL parsers use the same idea at larger scale.

Structure

interface Expression { int interpret(Context ctx) }

   AddExpression ----- left, right : Expression
   NumberExpression    (terminal)
   VariableExpression  (terminal, looks up Context)

 "a + (b + 2)"  becomes the tree:
          Add
         /      Variable   Add
     a       /           Variable Number
           b        2

When to use / when NOT to use

  • Use it for a small, stable grammar: rules engines, filters, formulas, simple query languages.
  • Use it when you must evaluate the same sentence many times, since the tree is built once.
  • Avoid it for big languages: dozens of classes and slow tree walking. Use a parser generator (ANTLR) or an existing engine like SpEL.
  • Avoid it when plain Java lambdas or a Map of functions already solve the problem.

Small program: boolean rule expressions

Here the grammar is tiny: variables, AND, OR. The tree for vip OR (member AND coupon) is built by hand and evaluated with different contexts.

expert.content:
Where Interpreter Pattern is Actually Used

  • Regex engines — a regular expression is compiled into a tree of terminal/non-terminal expressions and interpreted against input text.
  • SQL parsers — query language grammar (SELECT, WHERE, JOIN clauses) is parsed into an expression tree and interpreted/executed.
  • Rule engines — business rule engines (like Drools) interpret condition expressions such as "age > 18 AND country == 'IN'".
  • Spring Expression Language (SpEL) — @Value("#{someBean.someProperty}") is parsed and interpreted internally using this pattern.
  • Template engines — interpreting placeholders like {{ name }} in templates.

Terminal vs Non-Terminal Expressions

Type Meaning Example
Terminal Expression Leaf node of the grammar tree — cannot be broken down further NumberExpression, VariableExpression
Non-Terminal Expression Combines one or more other expressions to form a grammar rule AddExpression, MultiplyExpression, AndExpression, OrExpression

Why Interpreter is Rarely Used in Production

  • Performance: Deeply nested expression trees mean deeply nested recursive calls — this becomes slow for complex grammars.
  • Class explosion: Every grammar rule needs its own class, so a moderately complex language quickly results in dozens of expression classes.
  • Maintainability: Hand-written interpreters are hard to extend and debug compared to using a dedicated parsing tool.
  • Better alternatives exist: Real-world parsing needs (SQL, DSLs, config languages) are almost always solved using mature parser generator libraries like ANTLR, JavaCC, or existing libraries (e.g., javax.script, Spring's SpEL parser) instead of writing a hand-rolled Interpreter pattern.

When Interpreter Pattern IS still a reasonable choice

  • The grammar is very small and simple (a handful of rules).
  • The grammar is unlikely to grow significantly.
  • You need something quick and don't want the overhead of a full parser generator toolchain.

Interpreter vs Visitor Pattern

Aspect Interpreter Pattern Visitor Pattern
Purpose Evaluate/interpret a grammar or language expression Add new operations to an existing object structure without changing its classes
Where logic lives Each expression class implements its own interpret() logic Logic lives in a separate Visitor class, objects just accept() the visitor
Extending with new operations Hard - requires modifying/adding expression classes Easy - just add a new Visitor implementation

Interview Questions

#QuestionShort Answer
1What is the Interpreter Pattern?A behavioral pattern that represents grammar rules as classes and evaluates expressions using an interpret() method
2What is a Terminal Expression?A leaf-level expression in the grammar that cannot be broken down further (e.g., a number or variable)
3What is a Non-Terminal Expression?An expression that combines other expressions to represent a grammar rule (e.g., addition, AND, OR)
4Give a real-world example of Interpreter usage.Regex engines, SQL parsers, rule engines, and Spring's SpEL expression evaluation
5Why is Interpreter rarely used in large production systems?Performance issues with deep recursion, class explosion for complex grammars, and better alternatives like ANTLR exist
6Interpreter vs Visitor pattern?Interpreter evaluates a grammar/language expression tree; Visitor adds new operations to an existing object structure without modifying it

Real-time example 1: payroll formula engine with a parse cache

HR defines salary formulas as text, for example basic + basic * 0.4 - tax. The engine parses each distinct formula once, caches the tree and evaluates it for every employee. The printed parse count proves that the cache works.

Real-time example 2: boolean search query

A document search page lets users type java AND (spring OR boot) AND NOT legacy. A parser with one method per grammar rule builds predicates over the words of each document. This is the shape of the query parsers inside search tools.

Sample mini project: robot command language

A robot on a grid understands MOVE n, LEFT, RIGHT and REPEAT n [ ... ]. The program text is parsed into command objects (the grammar classes) and then interpreted against a robot context. Nested loops show why the tree structure matters.

Thread safety, testing and Spring notes

  • Thread safety: an expression tree built from immutable nodes (records, final fields) can be shared by many threads. Keep all mutable state in the context object, one per evaluation.
  • Testing: test each node alone, then the parser with a table of (text, expected value) pairs, including malformed input and operator precedence.
  • Spring: use SpEL instead of writing your own. new SpelExpressionParser().parseExpression("price * qty").getValue(context, Double.class). Use SimpleEvaluationContext for untrusted input so that method calls and type references are blocked.
  • Performance: parse once and cache; SpEL can also compile hot expressions to bytecode.

Anti-patterns

  • Hand-rolled mini language that keeps growing into loops, functions and variables. At that point use a real parser tool or embed a scripting language.
  • Executing user text with eval-style engines without sandboxing, which opens injection holes.
  • A single giant switch over token strings instead of grammar classes or a table of operators.

intermediate.content:
Arithmetic tree with variables and printing

WHAT: modern Java records as expression nodes. The same tree is both evaluated and printed.

WHY: the tree is data, so you can do many things with it (evaluate, print, optimize) without re-reading the source text. A Map acts as the context that supplies variable values.

Parsing text into the tree

WHAT: a small recursive descent parser that turns the text "2 + 3 * (4 - 1)" into nodes and evaluates it. One method per grammar rule: expression, term, factor.

WHY: the pattern itself does not parse text; a separate parser builds the tree. Seeing both together shows how precedence (multiplication before addition) comes from the grammar layering.

A rule engine for business conditions

WHAT: text rules such as "age >= 18 and city == Pune or vip == yes" are turned into condition, AND and OR expression classes and evaluated against a record of fields.

WHY: business users change rules often. With the interpreter, the rules live in data (a string or a database row), not in compiled code.

Postfix (RPN) interpreter with a stack

WHAT: a language with no brackets: "5 1 2 + 4 * + 3 -". Each token either pushes a number or applies an operator to the top of a stack.

WHY: for tiny languages a Map of operators replaces one class per rule, giving the same open-for-extension idea in far fewer lines.

Common mistakes

  • Using the pattern for a large language: the class count explodes and tree walking is slow. Switch to ANTLR or an embedded engine like SpEL.
  • Mixing parsing with evaluation: keep the parser (text to tree) separate from the expressions (tree to value).
  • Ignoring errors: bad input should raise a clear exception with the position, not a NullPointerException.
  • Re-parsing on every call: parse once, cache the tree, evaluate many times.
  • Evaluating untrusted expressions that can call arbitrary methods (a risk with SpEL and scripting engines). Restrict the context.
  • Ambiguous grammar: forgetting precedence rules gives wrong results such as 2 + 3 * 4 equal to 20.

Interpreter compared with similar patterns

PatternPurposeRelation to Interpreter
Compositetree of part-whole objectsthe expression tree is a Composite
Visitoradd operations to a treeuse it when you need many operations (print, optimize, evaluate)
Strategyswap an algorithmno grammar, one chosen algorithm
Commandrequest as an objecta script is often a list of commands run by an interpreter
Flyweightshare small objectsterminal symbols can be shared flyweights

interviewQA: What is the Interpreter pattern?

It defines a representation for the grammar of a language as a class hierarchy plus an interpreter that evaluates sentences by walking an expression tree. Terminal expressions answer directly and non-terminal expressions combine children.
Which design pattern does the expression tree resemble?
Composite. Non-terminal expressions hold child expressions exactly like a composite holds children, and a call on the root recurses through the tree.
When is Interpreter a bad choice?
For complex grammars. Each rule is a class, so the hierarchy grows large and slow to maintain. Use a parser generator such as ANTLR or an existing engine like SpEL instead.
Where does Java use it?
java.util.regex.Pattern, java.text.MessageFormat, Spring Expression Language, Jakarta Expression Language and JPQL or SQL parsing internals.
What is the role of the Context?
It carries the global information of one evaluation, for example variable values or an output buffer, so the expression nodes themselves stay immutable and reusable across evaluations.
How do you add a new operation such as pretty-print to an expression tree?
Either add a method to every node, or apply the Visitor pattern so that new operations (print, optimize, type-check) live in separate visitor classes without touching the nodes.
Does the pattern include parsing?
No. The pattern defines the tree and its evaluation; a separate parser (often recursive descent) converts text into the tree. Many descriptions blur the two.

topics.name: Iterator Pattern

beginner.content:
Iterator Pattern provides a way to access elements of a collection sequentially without exposing its underlying representation (array, list, tree, etc.).

Real-Life Example:

A TV remote lets you browse channels one by one using the "Next" / "Previous" buttons. You don't need to know whether the channels are stored as a list, an array, or fetched from a server - the remote just gives you one channel at a time.

Why do we need Iterator Pattern?

  • To traverse a collection without exposing its internal structure
  • To provide a uniform way of iterating over different types of collections
  • To support multiple simultaneous traversals of the same collection

Basic Structure:

  • Iterator - interface with hasNext() and next() methods
  • Concrete Iterator - implements traversal logic for a specific collection
  • Aggregate (Collection) - interface with a createIterator() method
  • Concrete Aggregate - returns a Concrete Iterator for itself

In one minute

The Iterator pattern gives you a standard way to walk through the elements of a collection one by one without knowing how the collection stores them. The collection hands out an iterator with hasNext() and next(); the caller never touches the array, tree or linked nodes inside.

More real-life analogies

  • TV remote channel button: "next channel" works whether channels come from cable, dish or internet.
  • Tour guide in a fort: visits the gates one after another; you just follow, you do not need the map.
  • Bookmark in a book: remembers the current position without changing the book.

Where you see it in Java and Spring

  • java.util.Iterator, ListIterator and Iterable (the interface that makes the for-each loop work).
  • Every Collection (ArrayList, HashSet, TreeMap.entrySet()) returns an iterator.
  • java.util.Scanner and StringTokenizer; Spliterator and Stream are modern relatives.
  • JDBC ResultSet.next() is a cursor style iterator over database rows.
  • Spring Data Page, Slice and Streamable iterate query results in pages.

Structure

interface Iterable<T>  { Iterator<T> iterator(); }
interface Iterator<T>  { boolean hasNext(); T next(); }

 FortList (Iterable) ---creates---> FortIterator
   [Raigad, Sinhagad, Torna]          index = 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> end

 for (String f : fortList) { ... }   // compiler calls iterator() for you

When to use / when NOT to use

  • Use it when you build your own collection or data source (tree, graph, pages from an API) and want for-each to work.
  • Use it to offer several traversal orders (forward, reverse, filtered) over the same data.
  • Use it to hide internal representation so you can change it later.
  • Avoid writing it for a plain array or list: the language already provides it.
  • Avoid sharing one iterator between threads; iterators hold position state.

Small program: a for-each friendly collection

Implementing Iterable<T> is all that is needed for the enhanced for loop. The iterator here is an anonymous class over a plain array.

expert.content:
Java's Built-in Iterator and Iterable

The JDK already implements the Iterator pattern via java.util.Iterator and java.lang.Iterable. Implementing Iterable in your own class lets it be used directly in a for-each loop, integrating naturally with the rest of the Collections framework.

Fail-Fast vs Fail-Safe Iterators

Java Collections provide two categories of iterators depending on how they behave when the underlying collection is modified during iteration.

Aspect Fail-Fast Fail-Safe
Behavior on modification Throws ConcurrentModificationException immediately Iterates over a snapshot/copy, no exception
Underlying mechanism Uses an internal modCount checked on every next() Works on a cloned/copy-on-write structure
Examples ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap

ConcurrentModificationException - Why It Happens

Fail-fast iterators (like those returned by ArrayList) track a modCount field on the collection. Every structural modification (add/remove) increments it. The iterator captures the modCount at creation and compares it on every call to next() - if they differ, it throws ConcurrentModificationException to warn you early rather than let the program silently misbehave.

Correct Way to Remove While Iterating

Real-time example 1: lazily paginated remote data

A client reads orders from a remote API that returns 3 records per page. The iterator fetches the next page only when the current one is used up, so memory stays small and no request is made for pages the caller never reaches. The fetch messages show the laziness. Spring Data and many SDKs use this design.

Real-time example 2: merging sorted log streams

Two servers write timestamped log lines in order. A merge iterator wraps both source iterators, peeks at their heads and always returns the older line, so you get one sorted stream without loading everything in memory. This is the core of external merge sort and of log aggregation tools.

Sample mini project: music playlist player

A playlist offers several iterators over the same songs: forward, reverse, only one genre, and an endless looping one that is limited by the caller. Small classes (song, playlist, iterators) cooperate and the program prints the listening order of each mode.

Thread safety, testing and Spring notes

  • Thread safety: iterators of ArrayList and HashMap are fail-fast and not thread safe. CopyOnWriteArrayList iterates over a snapshot (weakly consistent, never throws), and ConcurrentHashMap iterators are weakly consistent. One iterator belongs to one thread.
  • Resources: an iterator over a file or a database cursor holds resources. Use try-with-resources (an AutoCloseable iterator or a Stream) so that the cursor is closed even when the loop breaks early.
  • Testing: check empty collection, one element, many elements, NoSuchElementException at the end, and that two iterators over the same collection are independent.
  • Spring Data: repository methods can return a Stream or Slice to read big result sets lazily; always close the stream inside a transaction.

Anti-patterns

  • Copying the whole collection into a new list just to return an iterator, which wastes memory.
  • Index loops over a LinkedList (get(i) is O(n)), making loops O(n squared). Use the iterator.
  • Iterators with hidden side effects, such as hasNext() that consumes data twice or triggers network calls each time.

intermediate.content:
Generic collection with forward and reverse iterators

WHAT: a generic bookshelf that is Iterable<T> and also offers a reversed() view, which is simply another Iterable.

WHY: the client chooses the traversal order, and the shelf keeps its array private. The same idea is used by List.reversed() in Java 21 and by descendingIterator() in Deque.

Fail-fast iterators, safe removal and ListIterator

WHAT: three behaviors of the JDK iterators: removing inside a for-each throws ConcurrentModificationException, Iterator.remove() is the safe way, and ListIterator can go both directions and replace elements.

WHY: this is the most common iterator bug in real code and a favorite interview question.

Tree traversal iterator

WHAT: an in-order iterator for a binary search tree. It uses an explicit stack of nodes to remember where it is.

WHY: a tree has no simple index. The iterator hides the stack and gives clients sorted output with an ordinary for-each loop.

Lazy and filtering iterators

WHAT: an infinite Fibonacci iterator and a wrapper that filters any iterator with a predicate.

WHY: an iterator computes the next value only when asked. That makes infinite or very large sequences possible, and wrappers can be stacked, like decorators.

Common mistakes

  • Modifying the collection while iterating (except via Iterator.remove()) gives ConcurrentModificationException. Use removeIf or the iterator.
  • Calling next() without hasNext(): throw NoSuchElementException in your own iterator, as the contract says.
  • Returning the same iterator instance from iterator(): each call must return a fresh iterator, otherwise nested loops break.
  • Exposing the internal list through the iterator, so callers can modify it. Offer read-only views.
  • Sharing iterators between threads without synchronization.
  • Forgetting remove() support: the default remove() throws UnsupportedOperationException, which is fine if documented.

Iterator compared with similar approaches

ApproachControlNotes
