Iterator (external)caller pulls with next()caller can stop, skip, interleave several
forEach / internal iterationcollection pushes elementsshorter, cannot break easily
Streampipeline of lazy operationsone-shot, good for transformations
Visitoroperation applied to each elementseparates operation from structure, element types may differ
Compositetree structureiterators are often used to traverse composites

interviewQA: What does the Iterator pattern provide?
A uniform way to traverse the elements of an aggregate sequentially without exposing its representation. In Java it is Iterable plus Iterator, which makes the for-each loop work on any collection.
What is the difference between Iterator and ListIterator?
ListIterator works only on lists. It can move backwards (hasPrevious, previous), report indexes, and modify the list with set and add, while Iterator only moves forward and supports remove.
What is fail-fast and how does it work?

ArrayList and HashMap iterators compare an expected modCount with the collection modCount on each call and throw ConcurrentModificationException if they differ. It is a best-effort bug detector, not a guarantee against concurrency problems.
How do you safely remove elements while iterating?
Use Iterator.remove(), or Collection.removeIf(predicate), or iterate over a copy. Calling list.remove inside a for-each triggers ConcurrentModificationException.
Internal versus external iteration?

External iteration (Iterator) lets the caller control the pace with next(). Internal iteration (forEach, streams) lets the collection drive the loop, giving less code and easy parallelism but less control.
How do you make your own class work in a for-each loop?
Implement Iterable of T and return a new Iterator from iterator(). The compiler turns for (T x : obj) into calls to iterator(), hasNext() and next().
Why do CopyOnWriteArrayList iterators never throw ConcurrentModificationException?

They iterate over a snapshot array taken when the iterator was created; writers copy the array, so the snapshot never changes. The cost is memory and copying on every write, and the iterator does not see later updates.

topics.name: Mediator Pattern

beginner.content:
Mediator Pattern defines an object that coordinates communication between a group of other objects, so they don't talk to each other directly.

Real-Life Example:

  • Air Traffic Control Tower — planes don't talk to each other directly, tower coordinates them
  • Chat Room — users send messages through a mediator, not directly to every other user
  • Airport Ground Staff Coordination

Why do we need it?

  • Without a mediator, every object needs a reference to every other object (many-to-many mess)
  • Mediator centralizes communication logic in one place
  • Reduces tight coupling between components

Basic Structure:

  • Step 1: Create a Mediator interface
  • Step 2: Create a concrete mediator implementing coordination logic
  • Step 3: Colleague objects (e.g., User) hold a reference to the mediator only
  • Step 4: Colleagues communicate via the mediator, never directly

In one minute

The Mediator pattern puts an object in the middle so that other objects (the colleagues) do not talk to each other directly. Each colleague only knows the mediator, and the mediator knows the rules about who must react to what. Many-to-many links become many-to-one links, which are far easier to change.

More real-life analogies

  • Air traffic control tower: pilots never talk to each other, they talk to the tower, which decides who lands first.
  • Wedding planner: caterer, decorator and band coordinate through one person.
  • Group chat server: members send to the server, the server delivers to the others.

Where you see it in Java and Spring

  • java.util.Timer and ScheduledExecutorService coordinate tasks and threads.
  • java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService sits between the code submitting tasks and the worker threads.
  • Spring MVC DispatcherServlet mediates between request, controllers, view resolvers and handlers.
  • Spring ApplicationContext and ApplicationEventPublisher let beans interact without direct references.
  • javax.swing dialogs often use a controller class that links buttons, lists and text fields.

Structure

Without mediator:            With mediator:

 A <--> B                         A ---+
 |  \/  |                               |
 |  /\  |                         B ---[Mediator]--- C
 C <--> D                               |
 (6 links)                       D ---+   (4 links)

interface Mediator { void notify(Colleague sender, String event) }

When to use / when NOT to use

  • Use it when many objects talk to many others and the web of references is hard to follow.
  • Use it to reuse components: a colleague with no references to its siblings can be reused elsewhere.
  • Use it for UI form logic, chat rooms, workflow coordination and traffic control.
  • Avoid it for two objects only; a direct call is simpler.
  • Avoid a mediator that grows into a god object holding all the business logic of the system.

Small program: a tiny group chat

Users never hold references to other users. The chat room forwards each message to everyone except the sender.

expert.content:
How Mediator Reduces Coupling

Without Mediator, N objects that need to talk to each other require up to N*(N-1) direct references — a many-to-many mesh of dependencies. With Mediator, every object needs only ONE reference — to the mediator — turning the relationship into many-to-one.
codeExamples:
Without Mediator:                With Mediator:

  A --- B                           A
  | \\ / |                          |
  |  X  |                          M --- B
  | / \\ |                          |
  C --- D                           C, D

expert.content:
Mediator vs Facade

Both patterns introduce an intermediary object, but their purpose is different.

Aspect Mediator Facade
Intent Coordinates two-way communication between colleague objects Provides a simplified one-way entry point to a subsystem
Colleagues aware of it? Yes — colleagues explicitly call the mediator No — subsystem classes don't know Facade exists
Example Chat room, Air traffic control Simplified API over multiple complex services

Real-World Use — GUI Frameworks & Event Buses

  • GUI frameworks — a Dialog acts as mediator between buttons, textboxes, checkboxes, so widgets don't reference each other directly
  • Event Bus / Message Bus (e.g., Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher) — publishers and subscribers don't know each other, the bus mediates
  • MVC Controllers — often act as mediators between View and Model components

Common Mistakes

  • Letting the mediator grow into a "God Object" containing all business logic
  • Colleague objects still holding direct references to each other "just in case"
  • Not splitting mediator responsibilities when it becomes too large — consider multiple smaller mediators

Interview Questions

#QuestionShort Answer
1What is the Mediator Pattern?A behavioral pattern that centralizes communication between related objects through a single mediator instead of direct references
2What problem does it solve?Avoids a many-to-many mesh of direct dependencies between objects, replacing it with a many-to-one relationship to the mediator
3Mediator vs Observer?Mediator coordinates two-way communication between known colleagues; Observer is a one-to-many notification where the subject doesn't know what observers do with the update
4Mediator vs Facade?Mediator coordinates two-way communication colleagues are aware of; Facade simplifies one-way access to a subsystem the client is unaware of internally
5Give a real-world Java example.Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher acts as a mediator between event publishers and listeners
6What's the main risk of overusing Mediator?The mediator itself can grow into a "God Object" holding too much business logic

Real-time example 1: order orchestration with rollback

An order needs three steps: reserve stock, charge payment, book shipping. The services never call each other. An orchestrator (a mediator) calls them in order and, when a step fails, asks the earlier services to undo their work. This is the idea behind the saga pattern in microservices.

Real-time example 2: moderated chat with policies

The chat hub enforces rules that no user class knows about: muted users cannot post, banned words are masked, and every message is stored in a history for audit. Because all traffic goes through one place, new policies are added in one class.

Sample mini project: smart home hub

Four devices (motion sensor, lights, alarm, thermostat) never refer to each other. The hub translates events into actions: motion at night turns lights on, opening the door while armed rings the alarm, and a "goodnight" scene switches several devices at once.

Thread safety, testing and Spring notes

  • Thread safety: if colleagues run on different threads, the mediator is shared state. Use CopyOnWriteArrayList or concurrent maps for registrations, and keep each reaction short. Never call colleague code while holding the mediator lock.
  • Asynchronous mediators: a message queue or an ExecutorService in the middle turns the mediator into a message broker, with ordering and retry questions.
  • Testing: test colleagues with a fake mediator that records notifications, and test the mediator with fake colleagues that record commands. Because colleagues have one dependency each, mocking is easy.
  • Spring: the DispatcherServlet is a mediator; for your own code use a service or orchestrator bean, or ApplicationEventPublisher for loose coupling. Libraries such as Spring Integration and Camel provide full mediation routes.

Anti-patterns

  • God mediator with thousands of lines of if-else, replace it with smaller mediators or rule tables.
  • Hidden mediator through a global singleton, which makes tests and reuse hard.
  • Mediator that exposes colleagues' internals, so rules leak back into colleague classes.

intermediate.content:
Air traffic control tower

WHAT: planes ask the tower for the runway. The tower keeps the only state (who is using the runway) and queues the others.

WHY: the safety rule "one plane at a time" lives in one place. Planes stay simple and know nothing about other planes.

UI form with dependent controls

WHAT: a registration form with a checkbox, two text fields and a submit button. The button is enabled only when both fields are filled and the terms are accepted.

WHY: without a mediator every control would reference the others (the button asks the text fields, the checkbox asks the button...). With it, each control only reports "I changed" and the form mediator applies all enabling rules.

Auction house with bidders

WHAT: bidders place bids with the auctioneer. It rejects low bids, remembers the highest one and tells the previous leader that they were outbid.

WHY: bidders never know each other. Rules (minimum raise, who gets informed) can change in the auctioneer without touching bidder classes.

Multi-room chat with membership

WHAT: one chat server (the mediator) holds several named rooms. Users join and leave rooms and messages reach only the members of that room.

WHY: it shows that a mediator can manage groups and routing rules, which is what separates it from a simple observer list.

Common mistakes

  • God mediator: the mediator accumulates all business logic and becomes huge. Split it by area (one per dialog, per room, per workflow).
  • Colleagues that still talk to each other, which defeats the purpose and keeps the coupling.
  • Mediator holding strong references forever: colleagues that leave must be unregistered, like observers.
  • Circular notification: colleague A triggers mediator, which triggers A again. Guard with state checks.
  • Using a mediator where an event is enough: if no coordination rule exists, a simple Observer is lighter.

Mediator compared with similar patterns

PatternCommunicationKey difference
Mediatormany colleagues, one hubhub holds coordination rules, colleagues know the hub
Observerone subject to many observersone-way broadcast, no rules about what others do
Facadesimplified entry to a subsystemsubsystem classes do not know the facade, flow is one-way
Commandrequest as an objectoften sent through a mediator or bus
Chain of Responsibilityrequest passes along handlerssequential handlers, not a central hub

interviewQA: What problem does the Mediator solve?

It reduces the many-to-many dependencies between objects. Instead of every object referencing the others, each one references only the mediator, which contains the interaction logic. This makes the colleagues easier to reuse and change.
How is Mediator different from Observer?

Observer is a one-way broadcast from a subject to observers and defines no rules about what they do. A mediator coordinates two-way interaction between peers and encapsulates the rules about who reacts to what. The two are often combined: the mediator can use observers internally.
What is the main risk of the pattern?
The mediator can turn into a god object that knows too much and is hard to maintain. Keep each mediator focused on one interaction area and move reusable logic back into colleagues.
Give examples from the JDK or Spring.
ExecutorService and Timer mediate between task submitters and threads; Spring DispatcherServlet mediates requests, handlers and views; ApplicationContext events decouple beans.
How is Mediator different from Facade?
A facade gives a simpler one-way entry to a subsystem, and the subsystem classes do not know it exists. A mediator is known by its colleagues and they communicate through it in both directions.
How would you unit test a colleague?
Pass a fake mediator that records notify calls and assert the right events were sent. Since the colleague has only the mediator dependency, no other collaborators have to be built.
Where does a message broker or saga orchestrator fit?
An orchestrator is a mediator at service level: it calls services in order and triggers compensation when one fails, so the services themselves do not depend on each other.

topics.name: Strategy Pattern

beginner.content:
Strategy Pattern defines a family of interchangeable algorithms, encapsulates each one in its own class, and lets the client swap between them at runtime - without changing the code that uses them.

Real-Life Example:

  • A navigation app choosing between "fastest route", "shortest route", or "avoid tolls" strategies
  • A checkout page letting a customer pay by Credit Card, UPI, or PayPal - each is a different payment strategy
  • Java's own Comparator passed into Collections.sort(list, comparator)

Why do we need Strategy?

  • To eliminate long if-else/switch chains that pick behavior based on a type flag
  • To let each algorithm be tested, extended, and swapped independently (Open/Closed Principle)
  • To let the algorithm vary independently from the client that uses it

In one minute

The Strategy pattern puts each way of doing a job (an algorithm) into its own class behind a common interface. The object that needs the job (the context) holds a reference to the interface, so you can swap the algorithm at run time and add new ones without touching the context. It replaces long if-else or switch blocks that choose behavior.

More real-life analogies

  • Travel to the airport: walk, auto, metro or cab. The goal is the same, the way differs, and you pick based on time and money.
  • Payment at a shop: cash, UPI, card. The cashier (context) accepts any of them through the same step.
  • Navigation app: fastest, shortest, avoid tolls. Same map, different route algorithm.

Where you see it in Java and Spring

  • java.util.Comparator passed to Collections.sort, List.sort or TreeMap.
  • java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionHandler in ThreadPoolExecutor.
  • java.util.function interfaces (Function, Predicate) used as passed-in behavior.
  • javax.crypto.Cipher.getInstance("AES") and MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256") pick an algorithm by name.
  • Spring: PasswordEncoder implementations (BCrypt, Argon2), ResourceLoader, and injecting a Map<String, Service> of beans by name.

Structure

Context                         Strategy (interface)
+--------------------+  has-a   +---------------------+
| strategy           |--------->| execute(data)       |
| setStrategy(s)     |          +---------------------+
| doWork()           |                   ^
+--------------------+          +--------+---------+
                                |        |         |
                           StrategyA StrategyB StrategyC

When to use / when NOT to use

  • Use it when you have several ways to do the same thing and the choice depends on data, configuration or the user.
  • Use it to remove a growing if-else or switch that picks an algorithm.
  • Use it to isolate an algorithm so it can be tested alone.
  • Avoid it when there are only two stable variants that never change; a boolean is enough.
  • Avoid it if the client cannot understand the differences, since the client must pick the strategy.

Small program: choosing a travel mode

One interface estimate(km), three implementations, and a planner that can switch at run time.

intermediate.content:
Comparator as the JDK strategy

WHAT: the same list of employees is sorted three ways by passing different Comparator objects, including chained and reversed ones.

WHY: List.sort is the context and the comparator is the strategy. This is the strategy pattern you use every day without naming it.

Lambdas as strategies in a Map

WHAT: because a strategy is usually one method, a lambda replaces a whole class. Discount rules live in a Map from name to UnaryOperator.

WHY: less boilerplate and the choice is data driven. Adding a rule is one line, with no change to the checkout class.

Enum strategies

WHAT: each enum constant carries its own algorithm as a lambda passed to the constructor.

WHY: the set of strategies is closed and known, you get a type-safe list with values() and no separate classes. Good for tax slabs, operators and shipping modes.

Swapping a sorting algorithm

WHAT: a sorter context that receives either bubble sort or selection sort and reports how many comparisons each needed on the same data.

WHY: this is strategy in its classic form, an interchangeable algorithm. You could choose by input size (small arrays use simple sorts, large ones use faster ones) and measure objectively.

Common mistakes

  • Strategies that need data from the context but get it through ten parameters. Pass one small parameter object or the data itself.
  • Keeping per-call state inside a shared strategy object, which breaks when it is used by several threads. Make strategies stateless or create one per use.
  • Moving the if-else into the client instead of removing it. Use a Map, an enum or dependency injection to select the strategy.
  • No default strategy: a null strategy causes NullPointerException. Provide a null object (do nothing) or a sensible default.
  • Too many tiny classes for a one-line behavior. A lambda is enough.

Strategy compared with similar patterns

PatternVariesKey difference
Strategyan algorithm, chosen by the clientobject has one strategy at a time, no state transitions
Statebehavior depending on internal statestates switch themselves, the client does not choose
Template Methodsteps of an algorithm in subclassesuses inheritance, fixed at compile time
Commandan action and its parametersencapsulates a request (can queue and undo), not an algorithm choice
Decoratoradds behavior around an objectstacks wrappers, strategy replaces the behavior

expert.content:
Real-time example 1: pricing engine composing strategies

A shop calculates the final price with several independent strategies: a customer tier discount, a seasonal offer and tax. Each is a UnaryOperator chosen by data, and they are composed in order. Money uses BigDecimal to avoid floating point errors.

Real-time example 2: retry with pluggable back-off

A client calls an unreliable service. How long to wait before retry number n is a strategy: none, fixed, or exponential. To keep the program fast and predictable, the code records the delay it would sleep instead of sleeping. Real code would pass the delay to a scheduler.

Sample mini project: ride fare calculator

A ride app calculates a fare with a vehicle strategy (bike, auto, cab) and a separate surge strategy (normal, rain, peak). The booking class combines the two without knowing any concrete class. It prints a small readable bill for several trips in Indian cities.

Thread safety, testing and Spring notes

  • Thread safety: make strategies stateless or immutable so one instance can be shared across threads (Comparator and PasswordEncoder are). If the context lets callers switch the strategy at run time, declare the field volatile or use an AtomicReference.
  • Testing: test each strategy alone with plain unit tests (inputs to expected result), and test the context with a simple fake or lambda strategy. Contract tests can run the same cases against every implementation.
  • Spring: register each strategy as a bean and inject Map<String, PaymentStrategy>; the map key is the bean name, so strategies.get(type) replaces the switch. Use @Qualifier or @ConditionalOnProperty to select one by configuration, and List<Strategy> with a supports(request) method for rule-based selection.
  • Configuration: store the strategy name in config or a database row so behavior can change without a deployment.

Anti-patterns

  • Switch inside the strategy factory that grows forever: register strategies in a Map or let Spring discover them.
  • Strategy that knows the context's internals (passing the entire context object), so it cannot be reused.
  • Single-implementation interface created for hypothetical future needs, which adds indirection without value.

interviewQA: What is the Strategy pattern?

It defines a family of algorithms behind one interface, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable. The context delegates to the current strategy, so behavior can change at run time without changing the context.
Strategy versus State: what is the difference?

Both delegate to an interchangeable object. With Strategy the client picks the algorithm and it usually stays until changed. With State the object changes its behavior as its internal state changes, and the states themselves trigger transitions.
How does Strategy support the Open/Closed Principle?
A new algorithm is added as a new class or lambda; the context and the other strategies stay untouched. That replaces editing a long if-else every time a variant appears.
Name strategy examples in the JDK and Spring.

Comparator with Collections.sort, RejectedExecutionHandler in ThreadPoolExecutor, MessageDigest.getInstance by algorithm name, and in Spring the PasswordEncoder implementations and injected Map of beans by name.
How do lambdas change the pattern in Java 8 and later?

When the strategy has one method, a lambda or method reference replaces a class (Comparator, Function, Predicate). You still use the pattern, with much less boilerplate. Keep classes for strategies with state, several methods or their own dependencies.
How do you choose a strategy without if-else?
Use a Map from key to strategy, an enum whose constants hold the behavior, or Spring injection of a Map or List of strategies with a supports method.
What are the downsides of Strategy?

More objects and classes, the client must know the differences to choose well, and a single interface may force strategies to accept parameters they do not need. Do not use it for two stable variants.

topics.name: Command Pattern

beginner.content:
Command Pattern turns a request into a standalone object containing everything needed to perform an action (or undo it) - decoupling the object that invokes an operation from the object that knows how to perform it.

Real-Life Example:

  • A TV remote control - each button is a Command object that knows what device action to trigger
  • Restaurant order slips - a waiter writes a command that the kitchen executes later, independently
  • Undo/redo functionality in text editors

Why do we need Command?

  • To decouple the sender (the button/invoker) from the receiver (the object that does the actual work)
  • To support undo/redo by keeping a history of executed Command objects
  • To queue, log, or schedule requests as objects instead of executing them immediately

In one minute

The Command pattern wraps a request (do this, to that, with these values) inside an object. Because the request is now an object, you can store it, queue it, log it, pass it around, run it later, or undo it. The caller (the invoker) only knows one method, execute(). The receiver does the real work.

More real-life analogies

  • Restaurant order slip: the waiter does not cook. He writes a slip (the command), the kitchen (receiver) executes it later, and the slip can be cancelled before cooking starts.
  • Railway tatkal ticket queue: every booking request sits in a queue as a self-contained form, and counters process them one by one.
  • Smart-home scene button: one "Good night" button holds many small commands (lights off, fan off, door locked).

Where you see it in Java and Spring

  • java.lang.Runnable and Callable: a task object with one method. ExecutorService.submit(task) is the invoker.
  • javax.swing.Action / ActionListener: a menu item and a toolbar button share one command object.
  • java.util.function.Consumer and lambdas: a lambda is a tiny command.
  • Spring Batch Tasklet, Spring event handlers, and JDBC PreparedStatement (a command with parameters) follow the same idea.

Structure as text

Client ----creates----> ConcreteCommand(receiver, args)
                              |
Invoker ---- holds ---->  Command  <<interface>>
 (button, queue,           + execute()
  scheduler)               + undo()   (optional)
                              |
                              v
                          Receiver  (Light, Editor, Bank...)
                          + realAction()

When to use

  • You need undo / redo or a history of actions.
  • You want to queue, schedule or log requests (job queue, audit trail, replay).
  • You want to parameterise a button or menu with an action chosen at run time.
  • You need to group many steps into one macro action.

When NOT to use

  • The call is simple and direct, with no undo, queue or log. A plain method call is clearer.
  • A lambda or method reference already does the job and you need no history. Do not create ten classes for ten one-line actions.

Sample program: a queue of Runnable commands

The JDK already ships a command interface: Runnable. This program queues work first and runs it later, which is the heart of the pattern.

intermediate.content:
1. Undo and redo with two stacks

What it shows: a text editor whose every edit is a command that knows how to undo() itself. Why: the history is just a stack of command objects; undo pops from one stack and pushes on the other, so redo comes for free.

2. Macro command

What it shows: a command that holds a list of other commands (Composite meets Command). Why: one button runs a whole routine, and the macro can even undo the steps in reverse order.

3. Remote control with slots and lambdas

What it shows: a remote with numbered buttons, where each slot holds a command built from a lambda. Why: since Command has a single method, you rarely need one class per action in modern Java. Use classes only when the command needs undo state.

4. Command log and replay

What it shows: commands are stored in a list as they run, then replayed on a fresh object. Why: a log of commands is a cheap audit trail, and replaying it rebuilds state (the idea behind event sourcing and database redo logs).

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to store undo state. A delete command must remember what it deleted (and where) before it runs.
  • Sharing one mutable command object in several stacks. Create a fresh command per action.
  • Not clearing the redo stack after a new action, which makes redo restore a stale future.
  • Putting business logic in the command. The command should delegate to the receiver; otherwise it becomes a god class.
  • Unbounded history. Cap the undo stack (for example 100 items) in long-running apps.

Command vs Strategy vs Memento

AspectCommandStrategyMemento undo
IntentPackage a request as an objectSwap an algorithmSave and restore state
Typical methodexecute() / undo()compute(data)save() / restore()
Has a receiver?Yes, binds receiver and argumentsNo, works on given dataNo
LifetimeOften queued or storedChosen once, reusedSnapshot per step
UndoInverse operation (small)Not applicableWhole-state copy (large)

expert.content:
Real-time example 1: transactional batch with rollback

A fund-transfer batch must be all-or-nothing. Each step is a command with undo(). If step N fails, the runner undoes steps N-1 down to 1. This is a mini saga, and the same shape is used for multi-step order processing.

Real-time example 2: job scheduler with priorities

Commands in a PriorityQueue run in priority order, not arrival order. This is how task schedulers, print spoolers and notification dispatchers are built. The invoker never inspects the job; it only compares priorities.

Sample mini project: fort ticket counter with undo

Several small classes work together: a Counter (receiver), a booking command, a History (invoker side) and a main that drives a session. Read it top to bottom and notice that the history knows nothing about tickets.

Thread safety, testing and Spring integration

  • Thread safety: commands handed to an ExecutorService must be immutable or guard their receiver. Pass values into the constructor and never mutate shared fields without a lock. An undo stack shared by threads needs a concurrent deque or external locking.
  • Idempotency: if a queued command may be retried (message broker, scheduler), design execute() so that running it twice is safe, or carry a unique id and skip duplicates.
  • Testing: test each command with a fake receiver, and test the invoker with a stub command that counts calls. For undo, assert that execute() followed by undo() leaves the receiver as it started.
  • Spring: commands that need services are best created by a factory bean or by ObjectProvider; the invoker can be a singleton. @Async methods, TaskExecutor and Spring Batch steps all act as command invokers. Avoid making every command a singleton bean if it carries per-request data.

Anti-patterns

  • Command explosion: one class per trivial call. Use a lambda or a method reference instead.
  • Fat commands that contain the business rules instead of calling the receiver.
  • Undo by hope: expecting undo to work after partial failure without recording what was actually done.
  • Hidden global history as a static field, which breaks tests and multi-user apps.

interviewQA: What problem does the Command pattern solve?

It decouples the object that triggers an action (invoker) from the object that performs it (receiver) by wrapping the request in an object. That makes it possible to queue, log, schedule, pass around and undo requests.
How do you implement undo and redo with Command?

Give each command an undo() method that reverses its effect, and keep executed commands on an undo stack. Undo pops a command, calls undo() and pushes it on a redo stack. A new action clears the redo stack.
Where does the JDK use the Command pattern?
Runnable and Callable are commands, ExecutorService is the invoker, and the worker thread executes them. Swing Action and ActionListener are also commands.
What is the difference between Command and Strategy?
Strategy swaps an algorithm and usually has no receiver or history. Command packages a specific request with its receiver and arguments, so it can be stored, queued and undone.
What is a macro command?
A command that contains a list of other commands and executes them in order, so one trigger performs a routine. Its undo() runs the inner undos in reverse order.
When is a lambda enough instead of a Command class?

When the command has one method, needs no undo state and no extra behaviour. A lambda or method reference is then a lighter command. Use a class when you need undo, a description for logging, or serialization.
How does Command relate to Memento for undo?

Command undo stores the inverse operation, which is cheap but must be written per command. Memento stores a snapshot of state, which is simple but costs memory. They are often combined: the command keeps a memento taken before it ran.

topics.name: Template Method Pattern

beginner.content:
Template Method Pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class method, deferring some of its individual steps to subclasses - the overall sequence stays fixed, but specific steps can be customized.

Real-Life Example:

  • Making tea vs coffee - both follow "boil water -> brew -> pour in cup -> add condiments", but "brew" and "add condiments" differ
  • A standardized exam-checking process where the overall flow is fixed but subject-specific grading differs

Why do we need Template Method?

  • To avoid duplicating the common parts of an algorithm across multiple subclasses
  • To enforce a fixed overall structure/sequence while still allowing customization of individual steps
  • To let subclasses override only what varies ("hook" methods) - this is the Hollywood Principle: "don't call us, we'll call you"

In one minute

The Template Method pattern puts the fixed skeleton of an algorithm in a base class and lets subclasses fill in only the steps that differ. The base class owns the order ("first A, then B, then C"). Subclasses cannot reorder it; they only override the steps. A good rule of thumb: the base class calls the subclass, not the other way round. This is often called the Hollywood principle: "Do not call us, we will call you."

More real-life analogies

  • Exam paper format: every university paper has the same flow (instructions, sections, marks, submission). Only the questions change.
  • Building a house: foundation, walls, roof, finishing is the fixed order. A bungalow and a flat differ in the details of each step.
  • A bank loan process: apply, verify documents, assess risk, sanction, disburse. Home loan and car loan override only the verification and risk steps.

Where you see it in Java and Spring

  • HttpServlet.service() is the template. It decides between doGet(), doPost() and others, and you override only those.
  • java.io.InputStream.read(byte[], int, int) is built on top of the single abstract read().
  • AbstractList, AbstractMap and AbstractSet implement most methods using a few abstract ones such as get(int) and size().
  • java.util.Comparator.compare usage inside Collections.sort and TimerTask.run() are small variations.
  • Spring: JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate, TransactionTemplate (callback style), and AbstractApplicationContext.refresh() with its hook methods onRefresh() and postProcessBeanFactory().

Structure as text

AbstractClass
  + templateMethod()  [final]   <-- fixed order
        step1()                  (concrete, shared)
        step2()                  (abstract, must override)
        step3()                  (hook, may override)
        step4()                  (concrete, shared)

ConcreteA extends AbstractClass   overrides step2, step3
ConcreteB extends AbstractClass   overrides step2

Three kinds of steps: concrete steps (shared code), abstract steps (must be implemented) and hook methods (empty or default body that subclasses may override).

When to use

  • Several classes share the same sequence but differ in a few steps.
  • You want to avoid duplicate code by pulling the common flow up.
  • You need to control extension points so subclasses cannot break the order.

When NOT to use

  • Variations need to change at run time. Template Method is fixed at compile time by inheritance; use Strategy.
  • There is only one implementation. Extra abstraction adds noise.
  • Almost every step differs; then the skeleton is not really shared.

Sample program: exporting a visitor list

The base class fixes the order open, header, rows, footer. Subclasses decide only how a row and a header look. The final keyword protects the sequence.

intermediate.content:
1. Data import pipeline

What it shows: a fixed import flow (read, validate, save) where only the reading step differs between sources. Why: the validation and saving logic is written once, so every new source (CSV, JSON, Excel) is only one small class.

2. Hook methods

What it shows: optional steps with default behaviour. Why: hooks let a subclass add logging, skip a step or react to events without being forced to implement something. The abstract steps are the "must", the hooks are the "may".

3. A game turn

What it shows: the turn order of a board game is fixed; each game decides what "move" and "win" mean. Why: game frameworks use exactly this idea. The engine owns the loop and the game plugs in its rules.

4. Template Method with callbacks (the JdbcTemplate style)

What it shows: instead of inheritance, the template is a normal class that takes the varying step as a lambda. Why: it keeps the boilerplate (open, close, error handling) in one place and avoids a subclass per query. This is how JdbcTemplate.query and TransactionTemplate.execute work.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting final on the template method, so a subclass quietly changes the order.
  • Calling an overridable method from a constructor. The subclass fields are not initialised yet, which causes null pointer surprises.
  • Too many abstract steps. If subclasses must implement ten methods, the skeleton is too thin. Merge steps or use hooks with defaults.
  • Deep hierarchies. Three levels of template subclasses are very hard to follow. Prefer callbacks or Strategy.
  • Mixing state into the base class that is shared across calls, which breaks reuse and thread safety.

Template Method vs Strategy vs Factory Method

AspectTemplate MethodStrategyFactory Method
MechanismInheritanceCompositionInheritance
What variesSome steps of one algorithmThe whole algorithmWhich object is created
Chosen whenCompile time (subclass)Run time (swap object)Compile time (subclass)
Who holds controlBase class calls subclassContext calls strategyCreator calls factory step
Typical exampleHttpServlet.serviceComparatorCalendar.getInstance

Factory Method is often one step inside a Template Method.

expert.content:
Real-time example 1: servlet-style request dispatch

A web framework receives a request, picks the method, handles errors and writes a response. Application code overrides only doGet and doPost. This mirrors HttpServlet and Spring's FrameworkServlet, including the default "405 not allowed" behaviour of unimplemented hooks.

Real-time example 2: batch job with retry and audit hooks

Nightly batch jobs share a lifecycle: before, process each item, count failures, after. The template guarantees that the audit line is always printed, while concrete jobs only decide how to process one item and optionally how to react to failure.

Sample mini project: order processing for two channels

An online shop and a walk-in store both follow the same order flow. The template validates, prices, charges, ships and notifies. Each channel supplies its own shipping and notification, and the store channel turns off the delivery fee with a hook.

Thread safety, testing and Spring integration

  • Thread safety: a template object is shared by many callers only if it holds no per-call state. In the order example the log field makes the processor unsafe for concurrent use; in production return a local list instead of storing it in a field.
  • Testing: test the skeleton once with a tiny test subclass that records the order of calls. Then test each concrete step on its own. Hook defaults deserve one test each.
  • Spring: prefer the callback templates (JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate, TransactionTemplate, KafkaTemplate) over writing your own inheritance hierarchy. When you do subclass, mark the template final and register the concrete classes as beans; a service can then receive them as a Map<String, Processor> keyed by bean name.
  • Spring proxies: a final template method on a bean that needs a CGLIB proxy cannot be intercepted (for example by @Transactional). Put the annotation on the concrete steps or on a separate service.

Anti-patterns

  • Inheritance for code reuse only: extending a class just to reuse a helper, with no real shared algorithm.
  • Fragile base class: changing the order in the base class silently breaks every subclass.
  • Steps that call each other in a hidden order so subclasses must know the template's internals.
  • Empty overrides everywhere, a sign that the steps should be hooks or that Strategy is a better fit.

interviewQA: What is the Template Method pattern?
It defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class method and defers some steps to subclasses. The template method is usually final, so subclasses can change the steps but not the order.
What is the difference between an abstract step and a hook method?
An abstract step has no body and every subclass must implement it. A hook has a default body (often empty or returning true) and a subclass may override it to customise or extend behaviour.
What is the Hollywood principle?
High-level code calls low-level code, not the reverse: "Do not call us, we will call you." In Template Method the base class calls the subclass steps. Frameworks use it for lifecycle callbacks.
Template Method or Strategy: how do you choose?

Template Method uses inheritance and varies parts of an algorithm at compile time. Strategy uses composition and swaps the whole algorithm at run time. If you need to change behaviour dynamically or avoid deep hierarchies, use Strategy.
Give JDK or Spring examples of Template Method.

HttpServlet.service calling doGet and doPost, InputStream.read(byte[]) built on read(), AbstractList and AbstractMap, and in Spring JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate and TransactionTemplate, which handle the boilerplate and call your callback.
Why should the template method be final?
To guarantee the algorithm order. Without final, a subclass can override the template itself and defeat the purpose, which is to control the skeleton and expose only specific extension points.
What is the danger of calling an overridable method in a constructor?

The superclass constructor runs before the subclass fields are initialised, so the overridden method may see null or default values. Do not call overridable steps from constructors; start the algorithm from an explicit method instead.

topics.name: Memento Pattern

beginner.content:
What is Memento Pattern?

Memento Pattern captures and externalizes an object's internal state so it can be restored later - without violating encapsulation (no other object ever sees the fields being snapshotted directly).

Real-Life Example:

• A text editor's Undo feature - each save point remembers the document's exact content.
• A video game's checkpoint/save system - restoring a saved game returns the world to that exact state.

Why do we need Memento?

• To implement undo/redo without exposing an object's private internals to whoever manages the history.
• To let an object's state be saved and restored while keeping that state's representation private to the object itself.

The Three Roles

• Originator - the object whose state is being saved; creates a Memento and can restore itself from one.
• Memento - an immutable snapshot of the Originator's state at a point in time.
• Caretaker - stores Mementos (e.g. in a stack/history) but never looks inside them - it just hands them back to the Originator when asked.

In one minute

The Memento pattern lets an object save a snapshot of its own state and restore it later, without exposing its internals. Three roles work together: the Originator (the object whose state is saved), the Memento (an opaque, ideally immutable snapshot) and the Caretaker (keeps the snapshots but never looks inside them). The key idea is encapsulation: only the originator can read or write the memento's content.

More real-life analogies

  • Video game checkpoint: the game saves your level, health and inventory. Loading the save puts everything back exactly.
  • Bank passbook entry: a printed balance line is a snapshot of the account at that moment; it does not change when the account changes later.
  • Photograph of your desk before cleaning: if you cannot remember where things were, you restore from the photo.

Where you see it in Java and Spring

  • java.io.Serializable with ObjectOutputStream: the byte array is a memento of the object graph, and ObjectInputStream restores it.
  • java.util.Date.clone(), Object.clone() and copy constructors produce snapshots for defensive copies.
  • javax.swing.undo.UndoManager and StateEdit in Swing text components.
  • HttpSession attribute persistence, and Hibernate's "loaded state" array that it keeps to detect dirty fields (a memento of each entity).
  • Spring Web Flow snapshots, and database transaction savepoints (Connection.setSavepoint) are memento-like.

Structure as text

Caretaker  ----holds list of---->  Memento (immutable data)
    |                                  ^
    | save() / restore()               | created by / read by
    v                                  |
Originator  ---- createMemento() ------+
            ---- restore(memento)

When to use

  • You need undo, rollback or checkpoints and the state is easy to copy.
  • You must save state without breaking encapsulation (no public getters for every field).
  • You want named save points a user can return to.

When NOT to use

  • The state is huge and changes often; storing many full snapshots wastes memory (use Command with inverse operations or store only diffs).
  • The object holds resources that cannot be copied, such as open sockets or threads.
  • State is already persisted elsewhere (a database with history); a memento adds nothing.

Sample program: save and restore a volume setting

A small, complete example using a Java record as an immutable memento. The caretaker only stores it.

expert.content:
Why Encapsulation Is Preserved

The EditorMemento's state is only readable by the TextEditor (Originator) that created it - the History (Caretaker) only ever calls push()/pop() and never touches getContent() itself. This is the entire point of the pattern: the Caretaker can manage when to save/restore without ever knowing what is being saved.

In stricter designs, the Memento class is made a private inner class of the Originator, or its state-reading method is package-private - so only the Originator's own package can access it at all.

Memento vs Command Pattern

Both patterns are commonly used to implement undo, but they capture different things:

AspectMementoCommand
What it storesA snapshot of state (data)An action/request (behavior), sometimes with its inverse
Undo mechanismRestore a previous snapshot directlyExecute a stored "undo" operation, or re-derive the prior state
Best fitState is small/cheap to snapshot wholesaleOperations are naturally reversible (e.g. insert -> delete)

In real editors, the two are often combined: a Command represents "what the user did," while a Memento captures the state needed to reverse it cleanly.

The Memory Cost Tradeoff

Storing a full snapshot on every change can get expensive for large objects. Real systems mitigate this by:
• Storing diffs/deltas instead of full copies where possible.
• Capping the undo history depth (discarding the oldest Mementos).
• Using structural sharing (immutable data structures) so unrelated parts of the state aren't duplicated.

Common Mistakes

• Letting the Caretaker read or mutate a Memento's internal fields - defeats the whole purpose of the pattern.
• Making Memento mutable - a later change to the "saved" state would corrupt every restore point that shares it.
• Snapshotting far more state than is actually needed to restore correctly.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does Memento solve?Capturing and restoring an object's internal state (for undo/checkpoints) without exposing that state's internal representation to outside code
What are the three roles in Memento?Originator (owns the state, creates/restores Mementos), Memento (the immutable snapshot), Caretaker (stores Mementos without inspecting them)
How does Memento preserve encapsulation?Only the Originator can read a Memento's internal state; the Caretaker just stores and returns opaque Memento objects
Memento vs Command for undo?Memento restores by replacing state with a saved snapshot; Command undoes by executing a stored reverse operation - they're often combined
What's the main downside of Memento?Memory cost - storing many full-state snapshots can be expensive, mitigated with diffs or a capped history size

Real-time example 1: shopping cart checkpoint and rollback

Before a risky multi-step operation (applying coupons, then payment), the cart takes a checkpoint. If any step fails, the cart is restored so the customer never sees a half-updated total. This is the same shape as transaction savepoints.

Real-time example 2: spreadsheet cell history with a memory budget

A spreadsheet stores a snapshot per edit but only for the last few edits. Instead of copying the whole sheet, each memento stores just the changed cell (a small delta memento). This is the practical compromise for large documents.

Sample mini project: drawing canvas with undo, redo and named versions

A canvas stores shapes as immutable text records. The Canvas is the originator, Version the memento and VersionManager the caretaker with undo, redo and named versions. The program prints a readable story of a design session.

Thread safety, testing and Spring integration

  • Thread safety: take the snapshot while holding the same lock that guards mutation, otherwise you may capture a half-updated state. Immutable mementos (records with defensive copies) can then be shared freely between threads.
  • Testing: the key property is the round trip: save(); change(); restore(); must equal the original state. Add a test that mutates the object after saving to catch shallow-copy bugs, and a test that the history limit is respected.
  • Security and compatibility: serialized mementos should not be read from untrusted sources (deserialization attacks). Keep a serialVersionUID, and prefer a JSON or record based format for long-term storage.
  • Spring and persistence: an audit table or the Envers library for Hibernate keeps entity history in the database, which is a durable, queryable memento. In-memory HttpSession state should be small and serializable so it can be replicated across nodes.

Anti-patterns

  • Snapshot per keystroke of a huge object: store deltas or use Command.
  • Memento that holds live references to services, threads or connections.
  • Caretaker that edits the memento or reads private fields via reflection.
  • Using mementos as a database: long-lived history belongs in persistent storage with versioning, not in a static list.

intermediate.content:
1. Game save slots

What it shows: a caretaker that keeps named save points in a map. Why: unlike a simple undo stack, the player can jump to any earlier checkpoint, and the game class stays unaware of how saves are stored.

2. Undo and redo with a bounded history

What it shows: a history that keeps at most N snapshots and supports redo. Why: snapshots cost memory, so real editors cap the history. The pointer-in-a-list design also makes redo trivial.

3. Memento through serialization

What it shows: the originator writes itself into a byte array and reads it back. Why: this gives a deep copy of a whole object graph with almost no code, and the bytes can be saved to a file or sent over a network. Fields marked transient are skipped.

4. The shallow copy trap

What it shows: the most common memento bug. A snapshot that copies only the reference to a mutable list is not a snapshot at all. Why it matters: the "saved" state changes together with the live one, and restore appears to do nothing. The fix is a defensive deep copy when saving.

Common mistakes

  • Mutable mementos. If the caretaker or anyone else can change a snapshot, restore is unreliable. Use records, immutable classes or defensive copies.
  • Shallow copies of collections and nested objects (see sample 4).
  • Unlimited history. One full snapshot per keystroke will exhaust memory. Cap the size or store diffs.
  • Exposing the originator's fields through a public memento getter, which defeats the encapsulation that is the whole point.
  • Forgetting to snapshot all state, for example saving the text but not the cursor position.

Memento vs Command vs Prototype

AspectMementoCommand undoPrototype
StoresA copy of the stateThe inverse operationA template object to clone
Memory costHigh (full state each time)LowPer clone
Effort per featureLow, genericMust write undo for every commandLow
Best forCheckpoints, rollbackFine-grained editing historyCreating many similar objects
EncapsulationOriginator-only accessCommand knows the receiver APIClone method

interviewQA: What are the three roles in the Memento pattern?

The Originator creates a memento of its own state and restores from one. The Memento is an opaque snapshot, ideally immutable. The Caretaker stores mementos and hands them back but never inspects or changes them.
How does Memento preserve encapsulation?

Only the originator can read the memento content. The caretaker sees an opaque object (often a nested private or package-private class or record), so no extra public getters are added to the originator.
What is the difference between Memento and Command for undo?

Memento restores a saved copy of state, which is simple but memory heavy. Command stores the inverse operation, which is light but requires an undo method per command. Many editors combine them or use delta mementos.
What is the shallow copy problem in Memento?

If the snapshot stores references to mutable objects such as lists, later changes to the live object also change the snapshot. Take a defensive deep copy, or use immutable collections like List.copyOf.
How can you reduce the memory cost of many mementos?
Cap the history size, store only the changed fields (delta mementos), share unchanged immutable parts between snapshots, or snapshot only at meaningful checkpoints instead of every edit.
How does Java serialization relate to Memento?

Writing an object to bytes with ObjectOutputStream is a ready-made memento of its whole object graph, and reading it back restores a deep copy. Mark sensitive or runtime-only fields transient, and never deserialize untrusted data.
Where would you use Memento in a real backend system?

Savepoints inside a transaction, checkpointing a long batch job so it can resume, wizard or draft state before the final submit, and rollback of in-memory configuration when a reload fails validation.

topics.name: State Pattern

beginner.content:
What is State Pattern?

State Pattern lets an object change its behavior when its internal state changes - it looks to the outside world as if the object changed its class.

Real-Life Example:

• A Traffic Light - behaves differently in Red, Yellow, and Green states.
• An ATM Machine - behaves differently when a card is inserted vs when it isn't.
• A Media Player - Play, Pause, and Stop states each respond differently to the same button presses.

Why do we need State Pattern?

• Avoids huge if-else/switch blocks that branch on the current state everywhere in the code.
• Each state's behavior lives in its own dedicated class, instead of being scattered.
• New states can be added without touching any existing state class.

Basic Structure

• Step 1 - Create a State interface.
• Step 2 - Create concrete state classes implementing it.
• Step 3 - Create a Context class that holds a reference to the current state.
• Step 4 - The Context delegates behavior to whichever state object it currently holds.

In one minute

The State pattern lets an object change its behaviour when its internal state changes, so it looks as if the object changed its class. Instead of giant if / else or switch blocks that test a status field in every method, each state becomes its own object (or enum constant) that knows what to do and what the next state is. The object that owns the state is the Context; it simply forwards calls to the current state.

More real-life analogies

  • Traffic signal: red, green and yellow each behave differently, and each knows which colour follows.
  • Mobile phone profile: in silent mode an incoming call vibrates, in normal mode it rings. The same event gives different behaviour.
  • Courier parcel: booked, in transit, out for delivery, delivered. "Cancel" is allowed only in the first states.

Where you see it in Java and Spring

  • java.lang.Thread.State (NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TERMINATED) is an enum that models a state machine.
  • java.util.concurrent.Future behaves differently before and after completion; CompletableFuture has pending, completed and failed states.
  • Enum constants with their own method bodies (TimeUnit, RoundingMode-style design) are the modern, compact way to write State.
  • Spring: Spring Statemachine, Spring Batch BatchStatus and ExitStatus, and JPA entity lifecycle (transient, managed, detached, removed).

Structure as text

Context (TrafficLight)
   - state : State          ---- delegates ---->  State  <<interface>>
   + request()                                     + handle(Context)
                                                       ^
                          +----------------------------+-----------------+
                       RedState                    GreenState        YellowState
                      handle(): ... setState(Green) ...

When to use

  • An object has many modes and its methods are full of if (status == ...) checks.
  • The allowed actions depend on the current state (cancel only before shipping).
  • State transitions form a clear diagram that you want to see in the code.

When NOT to use

  • There are only two states and one or two conditions; a boolean is clearer.
  • The state is just data that does not change behaviour.
  • Transitions are driven by a large external rule set; a table or a workflow engine fits better than many classes.

Sample program: a traffic light using an enum

A compact beginner version. Each enum constant knows its own message and its next constant. No if chains appear anywhere.

expert.content:
State vs Strategy Pattern

State and Strategy look structurally identical (both plug an interface implementation into a context), but their intent differs:

AspectStateStrategy
IntentObject changes behavior as its internal state changesClient chooses which algorithm to use
Who switches implementationThe state objects themselves (self-transition)The client, from outside
AwarenessStates often know about each other / the next stateStrategies are independent, unaware of each other
ExampleATM, Traffic Light, Order statusComparator, Sorting algorithm, Payment method

Thread Lifecycle - A Real JDK Example of State

Java's Thread class is a great real-world analogy for the State pattern. A thread moves through states - NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED - and its allowed operations change depending on which state it's in, exactly like the ATM example.
• Thread.State enum represents the current state.
• The JVM internally manages transitions (you can't call start() twice, for example).
• The behavior of join()/interrupt() differs depending on the current state.

State Machine Libraries

For complex workflows (order processing, approval flows), hand-rolled State pattern classes can get unwieldy. Real projects often use dedicated state machine libraries instead:
• Spring Statemachine - declarative state/transition configuration for Spring apps.
• Squirrel State Machine - a lightweight Java state machine library.
• Enum-based state machines - using an EnumMap of allowed transitions.

Common Mistakes

• Putting transition logic in the Context instead of the State classes.
• Creating a new state object on every call instead of reusing singletons (as the ATM example does with hasCardState/noCardState).
• Forgetting to guard illegal transitions (e.g. requesting cash with no card inserted).

When NOT to Use State Pattern

• When there are only 2-3 simple states with trivial behavior - a simple flag/if-else may be enough.
• When states never change behavior, only data.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does State solve?Avoids scattered if-else/switch blocks by giving each state its own class, so an object's behavior changes cleanly as its state changes
State vs Strategy - what's the real difference?Same structure, different intent: State changes behavior driven by internal state transitions; Strategy lets the client pick an algorithm from outside
Who triggers a state transition?Typically the state objects themselves, by calling setState() on the context after handling a request
Give a real JDK example of the State pattern idea.Thread's lifecycle states (NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TERMINATED) - allowed operations differ per state
When should you avoid the State pattern?When there are only a couple of trivial states - a simple boolean/if-else is simpler and avoids unnecessary classes

Real-time example 1: circuit breaker

A circuit breaker protects a service from calling a failing dependency again and again. It has three states: CLOSED (calls pass), OPEN (calls are rejected fast), HALF_OPEN (one trial call decides). This is the idea behind Resilience4j and Hystrix. The sample uses a fixed list of call results so the output is deterministic.

Real-time example 2: support ticket with audit trail

A help-desk ticket moves through states, and every legal move is recorded with who did it. Illegal moves are rejected with a clear message. Business rules (only an agent can resolve, only the customer can reopen) are attached to transitions, which is how real workflow tools behave.

Sample mini project: train seat booking with waiting list

Each booking is an object with a state (WAITING, CONFIRMED, CANCELLED). A small Train class owns the seat count and promotes the first waiting passenger whenever a confirmed booking is cancelled. The states decide what "cancel" means for them.

Thread safety, testing and Spring integration

  • Thread safety: a transition is a read-modify-write on shared state. Guard it with synchronized, a lock, or an AtomicReference with compareAndSet(expected, next). State objects without fields can be shared singletons and are naturally thread-safe.
  • Persistence: store the state as an enum (@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)) and use optimistic locking (@Version) so two users cannot both move the same order.
  • Testing: test the transition table exhaustively: for every state and event, assert the expected next state or the rejection. A parameterised test over the full matrix is short and catches missing rules.
  • Spring: for non-trivial flows use Spring Statemachine, which supports guards, actions, hierarchical states and persistence. For simple lifecycles an enum with a transition table inside the domain class is enough and avoids a framework.

Anti-patterns

  • Boolean flag soup: isPaid, isShipped, isCancelled that allow impossible combinations such as shipped and cancelled.
  • God state class that handles every event for every status with a switch, which is the problem State was meant to remove.
  • States that call back into many context internals, creating tight coupling. Pass only what the state needs.
  • Skipping the audit trail for business workflows where "who moved it and when" matters.

intermediate.content:
1. Vending machine with state classes

What it shows: the classic State layout: one class per state, a context that delegates, and states that trigger transitions. Why: invalid actions (pressing "dispense" with no money) are handled inside the state that owns that rule, so the machine class has zero conditionals.

2. Order lifecycle with a transition table

What it shows: an enum for the status and an EnumMap that lists which transitions are legal. Why: when states carry little behaviour but the rules of movement matter, a table is shorter than a class per state and is easy to review.

3. Enum states with behaviour

What it shows: each enum constant implements the behaviour of its state (who can edit, what happens on "approve"). Why: you get the clarity of the State pattern without a separate interface and classes, and switch statements disappear. This is the form most used in modern Java.

4. States that return the next state

What it shows: a media player where every state handles an event and returns the next state, so the context never calls setState from inside the states. Why: transitions become pure functions that are easy to unit test and to print as a table.

Common mistakes

  • Keeping the old if/else inside the context as well as the states, so the logic lives in two places.
  • Allowing every transition. If any state can jump to any other, you only built a status field; write the legal-transition rules down.
  • Creating a new state object on every transition when states have no fields. Share them as singletons or use enums.
  • Hidden transitions scattered through business code that bypass the state objects.
  • State explosion: mixing two independent dimensions (payment status and shipping status) in one machine. Use two small machines instead.

State vs Strategy vs Command

AspectStateStrategyCommand
Who changes it?The object itself or its states, as events happenThe client, usually onceThe client creates one per request
Do variants know each other?Yes, states know the next statesNo, they are independentNo
Question answered"What mode am I in?""Which algorithm should I use?""What should be done?"
Typical useOrder status, connection, vending machineSorting rule, discount ruleUndo, queue, macro
Class structureSame shape as StrategySame shape as StateAdds a receiver and arguments

interviewQA: What is the State pattern?

It lets an object alter its behaviour when its internal state changes by delegating to a state object. The object appears to change its class, and conditional logic on a status field is replaced by polymorphism.
How is State different from Strategy?

The structure is almost identical, but the intent differs. Strategy is chosen by the client and strategies do not know each other. In State the object changes its own state over time, and the states usually know which state comes next.
Who is responsible for the transitions: the context or the states?

Both designs are valid. Letting states set the next state keeps the rules local to each state; letting the context or a transition table decide keeps all rules in one place and is easier to review. Pick one and be consistent.
When would you use an enum instead of separate state classes?
When states have no fields, little behaviour and are known at compile time. Enum constants can have their own method bodies, are singletons, serialise safely and work well with switch and EnumMap.
How do you keep a state machine safe with multiple threads?

Make transitions atomic: synchronise them, use a lock, or AtomicReference.compareAndSet. For persisted entities add optimistic locking with a version column so concurrent updates fail instead of corrupting the status.
What is wrong with boolean flags for status?
Several flags allow combinations that should be impossible and spread the rules over many if statements. A single state field with explicit legal transitions makes illegal states unrepresentable.
Give a real-world use of State in a Java backend.
Order lifecycle (new, paid, shipped, delivered, cancelled), payment status, circuit breakers, connection or session states, and Spring Batch job status. Thread.State in the JDK is a built-in example.

topics.name: Visitor Pattern

beginner.content:
What is Visitor Pattern?

Visitor Pattern lets you add new operations to a group of classes without modifying those classes themselves.

Real-Life Example:

• A Tax Auditor - visits different account types (Savings, Current) and applies different rules to each, without the account classes knowing anything about tax rules.
• A Shopping Cart discount calculator - "visits" different item types (Book, Electronics) and applies different discount logic per type.

Why do we need it?

• Adding a new operation normally means modifying every element class to support it.
• Visitor moves that operation's logic into a separate Visitor class instead.
• Keeps the element classes stable while the set of operations can keep growing.

Basic Structure

• Step 1 - Create a Visitor interface with a visit() method overloaded for each element type.
• Step 2 - Each element class implements accept(Visitor v).
• Step 3 - accept() calls back visitor.visit(this) - this is double dispatch.
• Step 4 - A concrete Visitor implements the actual logic for each element type.

In one minute

The Visitor pattern separates an operation from the objects it works on. The object structure (shapes, files, tax items) stays stable. Each new operation (area, price, export, print) becomes a new Visitor class with one visit method per element type. Each element has an accept(visitor) method that calls back visitor.visit(this). This two-step call is called double dispatch: the code that runs depends on the type of the visitor and the type of the element.

More real-life analogies

  • Tourist guide at a fort: the guide (visitor) treats a gate, a temple and a cannon differently, but the fort never changes when a new guide arrives.
  • Insurance agent: visits a house, a car and a shop and quotes a different premium for each, using one set of rules per visit.
  • Health inspector: checks restaurants, bakeries and sweet shops with the same visit, but looks at different things.

Where you see it in Java and Spring

  • java.nio.file.FileVisitor and SimpleFileVisitor used with Files.walkFileTree: the walker is the structure, your visitor decides what to do with each file or folder.
  • javax.lang.model.element.ElementVisitor and javax.tools / annotation processing; compilers and parsers (ANTLR, JavaParser, ASM ClassVisitor) use visitors over syntax trees.
  • Spring: BeanDefinitionVisitor (resolves placeholders in bean definitions), ASM ClassVisitor used by classpath scanning.
  • Java 21 offers sealed types with pattern matching for switch as a lighter alternative when all element types are in one place.

Structure as text

Visitor  <<interface>>                 Element <<interface>>
  + visit(Fort)                        + accept(Visitor v)
  + visit(Temple)                           ^            ^
       ^                                    |            |
  FeeVisitor, GuideVisitor               Fort         Temple
                                     accept(v) { v.visit(this); }

Call flow: element.accept(visitor) then visitor.visit(element). The first call picks the element class at run time; the second picks the visitor method.

When to use

  • The object structure is stable but you keep adding new operations.
  • The operation behaves differently for each class and you want the related code in one place.
  • You want to accumulate state while walking a tree (totals, reports).

When NOT to use

  • New element classes appear often: every visitor must then change. The pattern is good for adding operations, bad for adding types.
  • Elements are few and the operation is tiny; a simple method or a Java 21 switch is enough.
  • The visitor needs private data of elements, which pushes you to widen their public API.

Sample program: entry fees for places in a city tour

Two element types and one visitor. Notice that Fort and Temple know nothing about fees. A new visitor (opening hours, say) could be added without touching them.

expert.content:
Double Dispatch Explained

Java method overloading is resolved at compile time based on the static type of the argument - normally just single dispatch on the object a method is called on. Visitor Pattern achieves double dispatch - the method actually invoked depends on BOTH the runtime type of the element AND the runtime type of the visitor.
• First dispatch - item.accept(visitor) resolves by the actual runtime type of item (Book or Electronics).
• Second dispatch - inside accept(), visitor.visit(this) now has a compile-time-known static type for this (Book or Electronics), so the correct overloaded visit() is picked.
• This two-step trick is how Visitor simulates polymorphic dispatch based on two objects instead of one.

Open/Closed Principle - Adding Operations Without Modifying Classes

To add a new operation (e.g. a DiscountVisitor), you simply create a new class implementing Visitor. The Book and Electronics classes are never touched again - this satisfies the Open/Closed Principle perfectly for adding new operations.

The Tradeoff - Adding New Element Types Is Expensive

Visitor Pattern flips the usual extensibility tradeoff:
• Easy - adding new operations (just write a new Visitor implementation).
• Hard - adding new element types (e.g. a Furniture class) requires adding a new visit(Furniture) method to the Visitor interface AND to every existing concrete visitor.

So Visitor is best used when the set of element classes is stable/rarely changes, but the set of operations performed on them grows frequently.

Real Use - Abstract Syntax Trees (AST) / Compiler Design

• Compilers represent source code as an AST with node types like BinaryExpr, IfStatement, MethodDecl.
• Different phases (type checking, optimization, code generation, pretty-printing) are each implemented as a separate Visitor over the same fixed set of AST node types.
• This keeps each compiler phase in its own class instead of scattering logic across every node class.

Common Mistakes

• Using Visitor when element types change frequently (causes cascading interface changes across every visitor).
• Forgetting to implement accept() consistently on every element subclass.
• Putting mutable state inside the Visitor without resetting it between traversals.

Visitor vs Iterator

AspectVisitorIterator
PurposePerform a type-specific operation on each elementSequentially traverse elements without exposing structure
Adds new behavior?Yes, via new visitor classesNo, only traversal
Element type awarenessVisitor is aware of every concrete element typeIterator is unaware of element types, it just returns items

When NOT to Use Visitor

• When the class hierarchy of elements changes often.
• When there's only one operation ever needed - a simple method on the class is simpler.
• When the double-dispatch complexity isn't worth it for a small, stable set of operations.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does Visitor solve?Lets you add new operations to a fixed set of element classes without modifying those classes
What is double dispatch?Method selection based on the runtime types of TWO objects (the element and the visitor) instead of just one, achieved via accept()/visit() calling each other
What's the main tradeoff of Visitor?Adding new operations is easy (new Visitor class); adding new element types is hard (must update the Visitor interface and every existing visitor)
Where is Visitor commonly used in real systems?Compilers/interpreters operating on an Abstract Syntax Tree, where each compiler phase is a separate Visitor
Visitor vs Iterator - what's the difference?Iterator just traverses elements without adding behavior; Visitor performs a type-specific operation on each element it visits

Real-time example 1: file system tree with size and search visitors

Files and folders form a Composite. A SizeVisitor totals bytes and a SearchVisitor collects paths that match an extension. This is the same idea as Files.walkFileTree, with in-memory data so the output is stable. Folders pass the visitor to their children, so the traversal logic is written once.

Real-time example 2: one invoice, two export formats

An invoice has line items and a discount. Exports to a text summary and to XML are separate visitors that return a String. Adding a CSV or XML exporter later touches no invoice class. This is exactly how serializers and report engines are organised.

Sample mini project: payroll with several visitors

Three employee types and three visitors (monthly pay, yearly bonus, a text report). The employee classes carry data only. The report visitor also shows how to combine a visitor result into a readable table. Add a fourth visitor (for example "leave balance") without touching any employee class.

Thread safety, testing and Spring integration

  • Thread safety: stateless visitors (area, export to String) are safe to share. A visitor that accumulates totals is not; create one per traversal or per thread. If elements are mutated while visited, you need external locking or an immutable structure (records are ideal).
  • Testing: test each visitor with one small element of each type, and add a "recording visitor" that logs the visit order to test the traversal of composites. For sealed hierarchies the compiler already proves exhaustiveness.
  • Spring: visitors that need services can be registered as beans. A common idiom is to inject a List<Visitor> and run them all over a document (each visitor is one validation rule or exporter). Keep traversal in the domain model, not in a controller.
  • Evolution: expose visitor interfaces as a published API only if you can accept that adding an element type will break implementers. Default methods on the visitor interface (for example a visitUnknown) soften that.

Anti-patterns

  • Visitor for two classes and one operation: far more code than a plain method.
  • instanceof chains inside a visitor that defeat the dispatch the pattern provides.
  • Visitors that mutate elements in surprising ways during a read-only looking traversal.
  • Huge visitor interfaces with 30 methods that every implementer must fill. Split by sub-hierarchy or use an adapter base class with empty defaults.

intermediate.content:
1. Shapes with two visitors

What it shows: one set of elements and two independent operations (area and perimeter) implemented as visitors. Why: the shape classes stay small and never change when you add "draw", "export" or "scale" later. It also introduces a generic Visitor<R> that returns a value instead of printing.

2. Double dispatch explained

What it shows: why accept() is needed at all. Java picks overloaded methods by the compile-time type of the argument, but picks overridden methods by the run-time type of the receiver. Calling visitor.visit(item) directly with an Animal variable always chooses visit(Animal). Calling item.accept(visitor) first resolves the real class, and inside it this has the exact type.

3. Tax calculation that accumulates state

What it shows: a visitor with fields, walking a mixed shopping basket and building a tax summary. Why: the tax rules (5 percent on groceries, 18 percent on electronics, 28 percent on luxury goods) live in one class, and when the law changes only this class is edited.

4. Expression tree with evaluate and print visitors

What it shows: the pattern used on a recursive structure (Composite), the way compilers and calculators do it. Why: evaluation and printing are two separate operations over the same tree; each element's accept simply passes the visitor to its children through the visitor methods.

5. The modern alternative: sealed types and pattern matching
